# Fall River/New Bedford Line

The **Fall River/New Bedford Line** is a commuter rail line operated by the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA) in southeastern Massachusetts. Running from South Station in Boston to termini in Fall River and New Bedford, the line serves the South Coast region. It was established as part of the South Coast Rail project and officially began passenger service on March 24, 2025 , .

The line functions as a southern extension of the former Middleborough/Lakeville Line, which was renamed upon the commencement of service to the South Coast . The route utilizes the Middleborough Secondary, the Fall River Secondary, and the New Bedford Main Line to connect the region to the Greater Boston rail network . It is the first time since 1958 that the cities of Fall River and New Bedford have had direct passenger rail connection to Boston , .

## History

### Early rail service (1845–1958)
Rail service to the South Coast began in the mid-19th century. The Fall River Railroad opened in segments between 1845 and 1846, connecting Fall River to Myricks and eventually linking to the Old Colony Railroad for service to Boston . The New Bedford and Taunton Railroad began operations in 1840 . These lines were eventually consolidated under the Old Colony Railroad and later the New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad .

For over a century, these lines supported both commuter traffic and the "Boat Train," which connected with steamships sailing between Fall River and New York City . However, with the rise of the automobile and the decline of the local textile industry, ridership dwindled in the mid-20th century. The Old Colony Division, which served the region, ceased passenger operations on September 5, 1958, severing the rail link between the South Coast and Boston , .

### Restoration planning and Phase 1
Efforts to restore rail service to the region began in the 1980s . In 1997, the MBTA restored service as far as Middleborough and Lakeville on the Old Colony Lines, branding it the Middleborough/Lakeville Line . However, the extension to the major South Coast cities faced decades of planning, environmental reviews, and funding debates.

In 2017, the Massachusetts Department of Transportation (MassDOT) split the South Coast Rail project into two phases to expedite service. Phase 1 was designed to provide service via the existing Middleborough/Lakeville line using diesel-powered trains, while Phase 2 proposed a fully electrified route via Stoughton , .

Construction on Phase 1 began in 2019 . The project involved upgrading 36.1 miles of freight track for passenger use, constructing six new stations, and building two new layover facilities . The project missed initial completion targets of late 2023 and mid-2024 due to construction and testing delays , .

### Opening
The MBTA officially launched service on the Fall River/New Bedford Line on March 24, 2025 . The opening marked the completion of Phase 1 of the South Coast Rail project. To celebrate the launch, the MBTA offered free fares on the line through the end of April 2025 , . Upon the line's opening, the former Middleborough/Lakeville Line was officially renamed the Fall River/New Bedford Line .

## Route and stations

The line originates at South Station in Boston and runs southward along the Old Colony Main Line tracks, sharing stops with the Kingston and Greenbush lines as far as Braintree. From Braintree, it follows the alignment of the former Middleborough/Lakeville Line through Brockton and Bridgewater.

South of Bridgewater, the route diverges from the previous alignment. The former Middleborough/Lakeville station was renamed **Lakeville** and removed from the commuter rail schedule; it now serves only the seasonal CapeFLYER , . Trains instead proceed to a new **Middleborough** station located at 52 West Grove Street .

From Middleborough, the line utilizes the Middleborough Secondary track to reach **East Taunton**. At Cotley Junction, the line splits into two branches , :
* **Fall River Branch:** Diverges onto the Fall River Secondary, serving **Freetown** and terminating at **Fall River Depot**.
* **New Bedford Branch:** Continues onto the New Bedford Main Line, serving **Church Street** and terminating at **New Bedford**.

### Station list
The line serves the following stations , :

| Station | Municipality | Zone | Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **South Station** | Boston | 1A | Terminus; connections to Amtrak, Red Line, Silver Line. |
| **JFK/UMass** | Boston | 1A | Connection to Red Line. |
| **Quincy Center** | Quincy | 1 | Connection to Red Line. |
| **Braintree** | Braintree | 2 | Connection to Red Line. |
| **Holbrook/Randolph** | Holbrook / Randolph | 3 | |
| **Montello** | Brockton | 4 | |
| **Brockton** | Brockton | 4 | |
| **Campello** | Brockton | 5 | |
| **Bridgewater** | Bridgewater | 6 | |
| **Middleborough** | Middleborough | 8 | New station opened March 2025. |
| **East Taunton** | Taunton | 8 | New station opened March 2025. |
| **Freetown** | Freetown | 8 | Located on Fall River Branch. |
| **Fall River Depot** | Fall River | 8 | Terminus of Fall River Branch. |
| **Church Street** | New Bedford | 8 | Located on New Bedford Branch. |
| **New Bedford** | New Bedford | 8 | Terminus of New Bedford Branch. |

## Service and operations

### Schedule
As of the March 2025 launch, the MBTA operates 32 weekday trips between South Station and East Taunton. These split into 15 trips on the Fall River branch and 17 trips on the New Bedford branch , . Weekday trains run approximately every 70 minutes. Weekend service consists of 26 trips between South Station and East Taunton, with trains running every two hours , .

To facilitate connections, the MBTA operates shuttle trains between East Taunton and the branch termini (Fall River and New Bedford) for certain trips, allowing passengers to transfer at East Taunton rather than waiting for a direct train from Boston , .

### Fares
All stations south of Bridgewater (Middleborough, East Taunton, Freetown, Fall River Depot, Church Street, and New Bedford) are designated as **Zone 8** . As of 2025, the full one-way fare from Zone 8 to South Station is $12.25, with a reduced fare of $6.00 , .

### Rolling stock
Service on the line is provided by diesel locomotives hauling bi-level coaches, consistent with the non-electrified infrastructure of the Middleborough Secondary and the southern branches .

Railroad Depots of New Bedford’s Past


With all the speculation that the MBTA will extend the commuter rail line to New
Bedford (and Fall River), it seems appropriate to survey New Bedford’s rail history as
well as the buildings that once served as its terminal. The city has a distinguished past
regarding this indispensable metropolitan service. Two depots were constructed in
adjacent locations, near the site of the proposed new station.

The New Bedford & Taunton Railroad opened for business on July 1, 1840 to significant
fanfare which included many local and state dignitaries including the Governor. Joseph
Grinnell, the great man of vision who promoted and invested in nearly every civic
improvement of the day, was the driving force behind establishing the line. Other
prominent investors of the railroad included William Rotch, Jr, John Avery Parker,
George Howland, Jr and William W. Swain. The rails for the track were imported at great
expense from England but the line from New Bedford to Taunton was constructed in only
18 months. Regular service began on July 2 and included two departures and arrivals per
day. The branch line to Fall River was completed in 1876. Eventually, all the assets
passed to the Old Colony Railroad and then to the New Haven Railroad. When the
NHRR sold the station in the fall of 1959, passenger service ceased from the city.

The first train station built in New Bedford was the Pearl Street Depot, 1840 by Russell
Warren (1783-1860). Built in the very rare Egyptian Revival Style, it was referred to as
“the tombs.” (The Egyptian Revival was a style meant to evoke the grandeur of ancient
Egypt and was used extensively in cemeteries. It was used for other purposes but even the
most modest cemetery will have an obelisk monument in it.) The relatively small ticket
and waiting areas were connected to a long train shed that trailed behind the Pearl Street
façade. It was located on the north side of Pearl Street, east of Clasky Park, just before or
on the site of the Rte 18 downtown connector. Warren is the architect of many of New
Bedford’s important Greek Revival buildings including the Joseph Grinnell Mansion on
County Street, the Free Public Library Building on Pleasant Street, and the Rotch
Rodman House on County Street.

With the city growing rapidly, the old depot became obsolete and was torn down in the
1880s to make way for a large, modern facility. Because the steamboat wharfs were just
as important as the railroad for travelers, the depot was constructed closer to the
waterfront. This site was part of the harbor that was filled in. It was at the foot of Pearl
Street and on the harbor side of Acushnet Avenue. Eight trains each way to Taunton were
scheduled at this time as well as four to Fall River.

The new depot was opened on June 21, 1886 and was designed by Henry Paston Clark of
Boston for the Old Colony Railroad. It was a large stone structure that had an ample
ticket office and separate waiting rooms for men and women each with toilets and large,
open fireplaces. Other amenities included a telegraph office, cab or hack stand and
baggage facilities. It was a completely modern facility for its day.


Bibliography:

Berg, Walter Gilman, 1858-1908. Buildings and Structures of American Railroads: A
Reference Book. New York: John Wiley & Sons, 1893.

Boss, Judith A, and Joseph D. Thomas. New Bedford: A Pictorial History. Norfolk:
Donning Co., 1983.

                                                     Carrott, Richard G. The Egyptian Revival: Its Sources, Monuments, and Meaning, 1808
1858. Berkeley: University of California Press, 1978.

Ellis, Leonard Bolles. History of New Bedford and Its Vicinity, 1602-1892. Syracuse:
Mason, 1892.

Puryear, Thomas W. The Architecture of Russell Warren in the Coastal Towns of
Southeastern New England. North Dartmouth, MA: The Gallery of Southeastern
Massachusetts University, 1982.

Bruce Barnes, 02/06

March 25, 2025

South Coast Rail Service Officially Launches, Reconnecting Boston to New Bedford and Fall River
===============================================================================================

* * *

#### Categories.

[News](https://www.fmarchitecture.com/category/news/)

#### Tags.

[MBTA](https://www.fmarchitecture.com/tag/mbta/), [south coast rail](https://www.fmarchitecture.com/tag/south-coast-rail/), [new bedford](https://www.fmarchitecture.com/tag/new-bedford/), [fall river](https://www.fmarchitecture.com/tag/fall-river/)

* * *

![Image 2](blob:https://www.fmarchitecture.com/f9f8fb2cf578afd5bdf589d050326708)

Freetown Station

  

After decades of planning and anticipation, the South Coast Rail project officially launched on Monday, reestablishing passenger rail service between Boston and the cities of Taunton, Fall River, and New Bedford for the first time since 1958.

The Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA) commemorated the opening of the new Commuter Rail line with inaugural trains running from six newly constructed stations: Middleborough, East Taunton, Freetown, Fall River, Church Street, and New Bedford. The $1.1 billion project marks a major milestone in expanding public transit access and economic opportunity for southeastern Massachusetts.

As the architects of the new stations, our goal was to create facilities that both contribute to the character of their surrounding neighborhoods and promote a cohesive identity for the MBTA Commuter Rail system. Each station was designed with a focus on universal accessibility, forward-thinking sustainability and resiliency, and an emphasis on efficiency, durability, and low maintenance—ensuring long-term value for the communities they serve.

To encourage early ridership, the MBTA is offering free service from the six new South Coast stations through March 31. Weekend service will remain free through the end of April, including Patriots’ Day (April 21), and parking at these stations will also be free until April 30. The return of rail service to the region is expected to bring lasting benefits—including reduced highway congestion, increased access to jobs and education, and a boost to local tourism and development.

The List of MBTA Commuter Rail stations catalogs the over 140 stations comprising the [Massachusetts Bay](https://grokipedia.com/page/Massachusetts_Bay) Transportation Authority's (MBTA) [regional rail](https://grokipedia.com/page/Regional_rail) network, which delivers passenger service across 12 lines from Boston's [North Station](https://grokipedia.com/page/North_Station) and [South Station](https://grokipedia.com/page/South_Station) terminals to suburban and outlying municipalities in eastern [Massachusetts](https://grokipedia.com/page/Massachusetts) and [Rhode Island](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rhode_Island).\[1\]\[2\] This system, integral to Greater Boston's public transit infrastructure, facilitates daily commutes and regional travel, with routes extending westward to [Worcester](https://grokipedia.com/page/Worcester), northward to Lowell and Haverhill, southward to [Providence](https://grokipedia.com/page/Providence), and including recent expansions like the [South Coast Rail](https://grokipedia.com/page/South_Coast_Rail) to Fall River and New Bedford.\[2\] Stations range from major intermodal hubs with [subway](https://grokipedia.com/page/Subway) and bus connections to smaller flag stops, many featuring parking facilities, though accessibility and service frequency vary by line and location.\[3\]

Active Stations
---------------

### Stations Served from North Station

The [MBTA Commuter Rail](https://grokipedia.com/page/MBTA_Commuter_Rail) operates four lines from [North Station](https://grokipedia.com/page/North_Station), serving communities north and northwest of [Boston](https://grokipedia.com/page/Boston) along the Lowell, Haverhill, Newburyport/Rockport, and Fitchburg routes. These lines collectively include over 50 active stations excluding the terminus, with service frequencies varying by time of day and direction; inbound peak-hour trains typically run every 15-30 minutes, while off-peak service is less frequent. Accessibility varies, with many stations featuring high-level platforms compliant with the Americans with Disabilities Act as of upgrades completed between 2010 and 2023, though some remain low-platform or flag stops requiring passenger signaling.\[2\] **Lowell Line stations** (outbound order): West Medford, Winchester Center, Wedgemere, Anderson/Woburn, Wilmington, North Billerica, Lowell. This 25-mile route primarily follows former Boston & Lowell Railroad trackage, with all stations accessible except select flag stops; daily ridership averaged 4,200 in fiscal year 2023.\[4\]\[5\] **Haverhill Line stations** (outbound order to Haverhill): Malden Center, Melrose/Cedar Park, Melrose Highlands, Greenwood, [Wakefield](https://grokipedia.com/page/Wakefield), Reading, North Wilmington, Ballardvale, Andover, [Lawrence](https://grokipedia.com/page/Lawrence), [Bradford](https://grokipedia.com/page/Bradford), Haverhill. Wyoming Hill serves select trains but lacks full accessibility; several intermediate stops like Greenwood and [Wakefield](https://grokipedia.com/page/Wakefield) are flag stops outside peak hours, and the line shares initial trackage with the Reading stub. The full route spans 38 miles, with Haverhill as the endpoint since service restoration in 1973.\[6\] **Newburyport/Rockport Line stations** (outbound order, branching at [Beverly](https://grokipedia.com/page/Beverly_Farms)): [Chelsea](https://grokipedia.com/page/Chelsea), River Works ([flag](https://grokipedia.com/page/Flag) stop, not [accessible](https://grokipedia.com/page/Accessibility)), [Lynn](https://grokipedia.com/page/Lynn) (interim station during [North Shore](https://grokipedia.com/page/North_Shore) upgrades as of 2023), Swampscott, [Salem](https://grokipedia.com/page/Salem), [Beverly](https://grokipedia.com/page/Beverly_Farms); from [Beverly](https://grokipedia.com/page/Beverly_Farms), the Newburyport branch continues to [Montserrat](https://grokipedia.com/page/Montserrat) ([flag](https://grokipedia.com/page/Flag)), [Beverly Farms](https://grokipedia.com/page/Beverly_Farms) ([flag](https://grokipedia.com/page/Flag)), Manchester-by-the-Sea, West Gloucester ([flag](https://grokipedia.com/page/Flag)), [Gloucester](https://grokipedia.com/page/Gloucester), [Rockport](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rockport); the Newburyport branch to North Beverly, [Hamilton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hamilton)/Wenham, [Ipswich](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ipswich), Rowley, [Newburyport](https://grokipedia.com/page/Newburyport). This 41-mile (to [Rockport](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rockport)) or 39-mile (to [Newburyport](https://grokipedia.com/page/Newburyport)) line uses Eastern Route trackage, with [flag](https://grokipedia.com/page/Flag) stops requiring visible signaling and partial [accessibility](https://grokipedia.com/page/Accessibility) at coastal stations; service splits allow targeted runs to each [terminus](https://grokipedia.com/page/Terminus).\[7\] **Fitchburg Line stations** (outbound order to Wachusett): Porter, Belmont (flag, not accessible), Waverley (flag, not accessible), Waltham, Brandeis/Roberts, Kendal Green (flag, not accessible), Silver Hill, Lincoln (flag, not accessible), Concord, West Concord, South Acton, Ayer, Shirley (flag, not accessible), Groton (limited service), North Leominster, Fitchburg, Wachusett. Extended to Wachusett in 2016 with state funding, this 54-mile line follows historic Fitchburg Railroad path through Middlesex County; urban stations like Porter offer connections to the Red Line, while rural flag stops predominate westward, with accessibility concentrated at major halts post-2010s renovations.\[8\]

### Stations Served from South Station

The MBTA Commuter Rail lines serving South Station provide access to southern and western suburbs of Boston, as well as destinations in Rhode Island and southeastern Massachusetts. These include the Fairmount Line (an urban improvement line within Boston), Framingham/Worcester Line (extending to central Massachusetts), Franklin/Foxboro Line (to Norfolk County and Foxborough), Needham Line (to Needham and West Roxbury), Providence/Stoughton Line (to Rhode Island and Stoughton), Greenbush Line (to Scituate via the South Shore), Kingston Line (to Kingston via Plymouth County), and Fall River/New Bedford Line (to the South Coast region, with service commencing in July 2024).\[2\]\[9\] **Fairmount Line** stations (beyond [South Station](https://grokipedia.com/page/South_Station)): Newmarket, Uphams Corner, Four Corners/Geneva, Talbot Avenue, Morton Street, Blue Hill Avenue, Fairmount, Readville. This 9.2-mile line, focused on Dorchester and Mattapan neighborhoods, operates frequent service with level boarding at all stops as part of urban rail enhancements implemented since 2013.\[10\] **Framingham/Worcester Line** stations (beyond [South Station](https://grokipedia.com/page/South_Station)): Back Bay, Lansdowne, Boston Landing, Natick Center, West Natick, Framingham, Ashland, Southborough, Westborough, Grafton, [Worcester](https://grokipedia.com/page/Worcester). Spanning 39 miles to Worcester Union Station, this line carries over 10,000 daily passengers and includes express options, with full service restored post-COVID disruptions by 2023.\[11\] **Franklin/Foxboro Line** stations (beyond South Station): Back Bay, Ruggles, Forest Hills, Readville, Dedham Corporate Center, Endicott, Islington, Norwood Depot, Norwood Central, Windsor Gardens, Walpole, Norfolk, Franklin, Forge Park/495, Foxboro. This 54-mile line splits at Readville, with Foxboro service tied to Gillette Stadium events since 2008; it serves 7,500 weekday riders. **Needham Line** stations (beyond South Station): Back Bay, Ruggles, Roslindale Village, Bellevue, Highland, West Roxbury, Hersey, Needham Junction, Needham Center, Needham Heights. The 14-mile route, branching from the Franklin Line at Hersey, operates 28 weekday trains and connects to the Green Line D branch at Riverside (though not an MBTA Commuter Rail stop).\[12\] **Providence/Stoughton Line** stations (beyond [South Station](https://grokipedia.com/page/South_Station), mainline to [Providence](https://grokipedia.com/page/Providence)): Back Bay, Route 128, [Canton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Canton) Central, [Canton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Canton) Junction, [Sharon](https://grokipedia.com/page/Sharon), [Mansfield](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mansfield), Attleboro, South Attleboro, Pawtucket/Central Falls, [Providence](https://grokipedia.com/page/Providence), T.F. Green Airport, [Wickford](https://grokipedia.com/page/Wickford) Junction. Stoughton branch (from [Canton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Canton) Junction): Stoughton. This 52-mile interstate line, extended to [Wickford](https://grokipedia.com/page/Wickford) in 2012, averages 40-minute run times to [Providence](https://grokipedia.com/page/Providence) with [Amtrak](https://grokipedia.com/page/Amtrak) interlining.\[13\] **Greenbush Line** stations (beyond [South Station](https://grokipedia.com/page/South_Station)): JFK/UMass, Quincy Center, Weymouth Landing/East Braintree, East Weymouth, West Hingham, Nantasket Junction, Cohasset, North Scituate, Greenbush. The 26-mile South Shore route, reopened in 2007, shares trackage with the Kingston Line to Braintree and serves Cohasset beaches.\[14\] **Kingston Line** stations (beyond South Station): JFK/UMass, Quincy Center, Braintree, South Weymouth, Abington, Whitman, [Hanson](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hanson), [Halifax](https://grokipedia.com/page/Halifax), Kingston. This 34-mile line, part of the [Old Colony Railroad](https://grokipedia.com/page/Old_Colony_Railroad) restoration in 1995, previously extended to [Plymouth](https://grokipedia.com/page/Plymouth) until 2021; it handles seasonal demand to [Cape Cod](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cape_Cod) gateways.\[15\] **Fall River/New Bedford Line** stations (beyond South Station): JFK/UMass, Quincy Center, Braintree, Bridgewater, Middleborough, East Taunton; Fall River branch: [Freetown](https://grokipedia.com/page/Freetown), Fall River Depot; New Bedford branch: Westport, New Bedford. Launched in 2024 as Phase 1 of [South Coast Rail](https://grokipedia.com/page/South_Coast_Rail), this 60-mile service uses upgraded legacy trackage to Middleborough with six new stations, projecting 4,700 daily boardings upon full electrification.\[16\]\[9\]

Planned Stations
----------------

### Stations Under Construction

As of October 2025, no new MBTA Commuter Rail stations are under construction. The MBTA's ongoing projects focus primarily on maintenance yards, accessibility upgrades to existing stations, and infrastructure repairs rather than new passenger facilities.\[17\] For instance, recent completions include the [South Coast Rail](https://grokipedia.com/page/South_Coast_Rail) Phase 1, which opened service on March 24, 2025, adding six stations along the Fall River/New Bedford Line from Middleborough/Lakeville to New Bedford and Fall River.\[18\] \[9\] The North Wilmington station on the [Lowell Line](https://grokipedia.com/page/Lowell_Line) also entered passenger service on June 30, 2025, following construction completion.\[19\] Future station developments, such as [South Coast Rail](https://grokipedia.com/page/South_Coast_Rail) Phase 2 extensions, remain in planning without active construction or funding secured.\[9\]

### Proposed Expansions

The MBTA has evaluated several proposals for new [infill](https://grokipedia.com/page/Infill) stations on existing [Commuter Rail](https://grokipedia.com/page/Commuter_rail) lines to improve access and support regional development. One such proposal is the West Station on the [Framingham/Worcester Line](https://grokipedia.com/page/Framingham/Worcester_Line) in Boston's [Allston](https://grokipedia.com/page/Allston) neighborhood, intended to serve the area's growing population and connect with the [Massachusetts Turnpike](https://grokipedia.com/page/Massachusetts_Turnpike) interchange as part of the Allston Multimodal Project and I-90 viaduct reconstruction. This station would feature platforms integrated with viaduct improvements, potentially enabling higher frequencies under the [Regional Rail](https://grokipedia.com/page/Regional_rail) modernization efforts, though detailed design and funding remain pending as of 2024 planning discussions.\[20\] Line extensions beyond current termini represent longer-term proposals, often tied to state studies assessing feasibility and ridership. The East-West Passenger Rail Study, completed by MassDOT in coordination with [Amtrak](https://grokipedia.com/page/Amtrak) and regional stakeholders, outlines options for enhanced diesel or electrified service from [Boston](https://grokipedia.com/page/Boston) through [Worcester](https://grokipedia.com/page/Worcester) to [Springfield](https://grokipedia.com/page/Springfield) and Pittsfield, including potential new intermediate stations to boost connectivity along the corridor. These could extend [MBTA Commuter Rail](https://grokipedia.com/page/MBTA_Commuter_Rail) operations or integrate with intercity services, with estimated costs exceeding $2 billion for infrastructure upgrades like additional tracks and signaling; however, implementation depends on federal funding and environmental reviews, with no construction timeline set as of the study's 2022 final report.\[21\] Other infill proposals, such as a potential station on the Needham Line near [Millennium Park](https://grokipedia.com/page/Millennium_Park) in [West Roxbury](https://grokipedia.com/page/West_Roxbury), have been explored by the City of [Boston](https://grokipedia.com/page/Boston) for improved local access, but lack committed state funding or MBTA endorsement beyond preliminary feasibility assessments. These initiatives align with the MBTA's Focus40 long-range plan, which emphasizes service reliability over rapid expansion, prioritizing [electrification](https://grokipedia.com/page/Electrification) and [frequency](https://grokipedia.com/page/Frequency) increases on core routes before new station builds.\[22\]

Former Stations
---------------

### Stations Closed Prior to MBTA Subsidies

Prior to the MBTA's commencement of [commuter rail](https://grokipedia.com/page/Commuter_rail) subsidies in stages beginning in 1965, private railroads operating in the [Boston](https://grokipedia.com/page/Boston) area closed numerous stations as ridership declined sharply after [World War II](https://grokipedia.com/page/World_War_II) and operating losses mounted, prompting cost-cutting measures independent of public funding.\[23\] These closures affected lines later incorporated into the MBTA system, with operators like the Boston & Maine (B&M) and New York, New Haven and Hartford (NYNH&H) eliminating low-patronage stops to streamline service and reduce expenses.\[24\] The most significant pre-subsidy closure event involved the NYNH&H's Old Colony Division, where passenger service on branches to [Plymouth](https://grokipedia.com/page/Plymouth), Kingston, Middleborough, and other South Shore destinations ended on July 8, 1958, shuttering dozens of stations amid ongoing financial distress for the railroad.\[25\] This discontinuation, upheld after temporary resumption due to legal challenges, reflected broader trends of branch-line abandonment, though through service to [Providence](https://grokipedia.com/page/Providence) persisted until later integration.\[26\] The [B&M](https://grokipedia.com/page/B&M), struggling with profitability in the late 1950s, closed its dedicated passenger station in Lowell on September 7, 1959, consolidating operations as part of dieselization and service rationalization efforts.\[27\] Similar reductions occurred on [B&M](https://grokipedia.com/page/B&M) lines, including the elimination of many inner-suburban stops within the pre-existing Metropolitan Transit Authority district boundaries, though exact counts varied by route.\[24\] These actions preceded state intervention, leaving a reduced network of primarily express and high-volume stations when subsidies initiated.

### Stations Closed After MBTA Subsidies Began

Despite the onset of state subsidies for [commuter rail](https://grokipedia.com/page/Commuter_rail) in 1965, the MBTA pursued further service rationalization, closing dozens of low-volume stations through the [1970s](https://grokipedia.com/page/1970s) and into the early [1980s](https://grokipedia.com/page/1980s) to mitigate operating deficits and concentrate resources on busier segments.\[23\] These decisions were influenced by persistent ridership declines, escalating maintenance expenses on aging infrastructure, and fiscal pressures that limited the subsidies' ability to sustain marginal stops.\[28\] Key examples include the truncation of the Central Massachusetts Branch, where South Sudbury station lost regular passenger service in 1971 amid inadequate demand for extension beyond that point.\[28\] Similarly, the [Bedford](https://grokipedia.com/page/Bedford) Branch ceased operations in 1981, following a 1977 snowstorm that rendered tracks impassable and underscored the line's underutilization, with too few riders to warrant costly upgrades.\[29\] On the [Lowell Line](https://grokipedia.com/page/Lowell_Line), Clematis Brook and Beaver Brook stations were eliminated in 1978 as part of incremental cuts to underpatronized flag stops.\[30\] Salem Street station on the same line had closed earlier, in October 1967, reflecting early post-subsidy adjustments.\[30\] Such closures, while reducing the network's footprint, preserved viability for subsidized core services; however, they also contributed to automobile dependency in outer suburbs, as alternative transit options were limited.\[28\] By the mid-1980s, [expansion](https://grokipedia.com/page/Expansion) efforts began to reverse some trends, but the pre-1980s stations remain shuttered without reopening.\[23\]

### Relocated or Replaced Stations

Several [MBTA Commuter Rail](https://grokipedia.com/page/MBTA_Commuter_Rail) stations have been relocated or replaced to improve accessibility, accommodate infrastructure upgrades, or better align with service expansions. These changes typically involve constructing new platforms at slightly different locations along the line, rendering the original sites obsolete for regular service.\[9\] The former Middleborough/Lakeville [station](https://grokipedia.com/page/Station) on the Middleborough/Lakeville Line was replaced by a new Middleborough [station](https://grokipedia.com/page/Station) approximately 0.7 miles (1.1 km) to the north in 2025 as part of the [South Coast Rail](https://grokipedia.com/page/South_Coast_Rail) project, which extends service to New Bedford and Fall River. The original [station](https://grokipedia.com/page/Station) site was renamed Lakeville and retained for limited seasonal [CapeFLYER](https://grokipedia.com/page/CapeFlyer) service.\[9\] Chelsea station on the Newburyport/Rockport Line was replaced in November 2021 with a new facility on Everett Avenue, approximately 0.3 miles west of the original Arlington Street location, to enhance connections with the Silver Line and improve accessibility. The prior station, dating to the early [20th century](https://grokipedia.com/page/20th_century), was demolished following the relocation.\[31\]\[32\] North Wilmington station on the [Haverhill Line](https://grokipedia.com/page/Haverhill_Line) saw its original low [platform](https://grokipedia.com/page/Platform) demolished in early 2025 and replaced by a new accessible station on Middlesex Avenue, which opened on June 30, 2025, featuring level boarding ramps and expanded parking. This upgrade addressed longstanding accessibility deficiencies at the site, operational since the 1970s.\[33\]\[34\] Salem station on the Newburyport/Rockport Line was relocated in 1987 to a new site south of the original depot to facilitate track improvements and better serve growing ridership, with the move involving a shift of about 0.5 miles along the right-of-way.\[35\]

MBTA Regional Rail Service Has Arrived In Fall River and New Bedford
====================================================================

"The platform was packed. A lot of people were taking pictures and videos. And then there were some people for whom it was just another workday," a rider on the first train told StreetsblogMASS.

[![Image 3](https://lede-admin.mass.streetsblog.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/49/2023/05/PROMO-milneil.png?resize=100%2C100)](https://mass.streetsblog.org/author/christianmilneil)

By [Christian MilNeil](https://mass.streetsblog.org/author/christianmilneil)

11:05 AM EDT on March 24, 2025

*   [Share on Reddit](http://www.reddit.com/submit/?title=MBTA%20Regional%20Rail%20Service%20Has%20Arrived%20In%20Fall%20River%20and%20New%20Bedford&url=https%3A%2F%2Fmass.streetsblog.org%2F2025%2F03%2F24%2Fmbta-regional-rail-service-has-arrived-in-fall-river-and-new-bedford)

*   [Share on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle/?summary=After%20decades%20of%20planning%20followed%20by%20years%20of%20delays%20in%20the%20wake%20of%20the%20Covid-19%20pandemic%2C%20the%20MBTA%26%238217%3Bs%20South%20Coast%20Rail%20project%20opened%20this%20morning%20as%20the%20first%20MBTA%20regional%20rail%20trains%20departed%20from%20new%20stations%20in%20Fall%20River%2C%20New%20Bedford%2C%20and%20East%20Taunton.%20Dozens%20of%20transit%20enthusiasts%20and%20commuters%20crowded%20the%20platform%20of%20the%E2%80%A6%0A&title=MBTA%20Regional%20Rail%20Service%20Has%20Arrived%20In%20Fall%20River%20and%20New%20Bedford&url=https%3A%2F%2Fmass.streetsblog.org%2F2025%2F03%2F24%2Fmbta-regional-rail-service-has-arrived-in-fall-river-and-new-bedford)
*   [Share on Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fmass.streetsblog.org%2F2025%2F03%2F24%2Fmbta-regional-rail-service-has-arrived-in-fall-river-and-new-bedford)
*   [Share on Email](mailto:?body=https%3A%2F%2Fmass.streetsblog.org%2F2025%2F03%2F24%2Fmbta-regional-rail-service-has-arrived-in-fall-river-and-new-bedford&subject=MBTA%20Regional%20Rail%20Service%20Has%20Arrived%20In%20Fall%20River%20and%20New%20Bedford)

![Image 4: A crowd of passengers on a lit train platform under a dark sky, with a purple MBTA commuter rail train at right.](https://lede-admin.mass.streetsblog.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/49/2025/03/New-Bedford-inaugural-South-Coast-Rail-train-03.24.2025-credit-Dan-Brogan.jpeg?w=2880)

The first MBTA regional rail train to carry passengers arrives at the platform in New Bedford early Monday morning, March 24, 2025. Photo courtesy of Dan Brogan.

After decades of planning followed by years of delays in the wake of the Covid-19 pandemic, the MBTA's South Coast Rail project opened this morning as the first MBTA regional rail trains departed from new stations in Fall River, New Bedford, and East Taunton.

Dozens of transit enthusiasts and commuters crowded the platform of the New Bedford station in the darkness this morning to catch the first 4:27 a.m. train towards Boston.

Among the first passengers on that first train was New Bedford resident Jacob Hoss, who says he's been waiting patiently for the new line to open ever since he moved to New Bedford 15 years ago.

"The platform was packed. A lot of people were taking pictures and videos. And then there were some people for whom it was just another workday," Hoss told StreetsblogMASS.

![Image 5: A stylized rail map of the MBTA Fall River/New Bedford Line, with South Station at the top, Braintree in the center, and Fall River in the lower left corner, and New Bedford in the lower edge.](https://lede-admin.mass.streetsblog.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/49/2025/03/2025-03-04-fall-river-new-bedford-line-map.png?w=710)

A diagram of the new Fall River/New Bedford regional rail line. Courtesy of the MBTA.

"It’s a mix of typical early morning, pre-dawn commuters – quite a few people are taking a nap – but there are a lot of transit enthusiasts on the train, a lot of people seem excited," added Hoss. "I’m riding with my girlfriend who just moved here from Buffalo – she works at one of the colleges in Boston, so she’ll be taking this train almost every day."

A long wait
-----------

The last passenger trains to serve New Bedford and Fall River operated under the private New Haven Railroad, which ended service to the cities in 1958.

South coast politicians began advocating for the MBTA to bring back commuter rail service to the region in the 1980s, [and after several false starts](https://newbedfordlight.org/key-points-on-the-route-to-south-coast-rail/), construction work began in earnest in 2019.

[At a groundbreaking ceremony that year](https://www.vhb.com/news/MBTA-South-Coast-Rail-Project-Breaks-Ground/), Governor Charlie Baker told reporters that the new rail line would be open before the end of 2023.

The T initially [pushed that date back into the summer of 2024](https://fallriverreporter.com/south-coast-rail-now-expected-to-be-ready-next-summer/#:~:text=During%20a%20wide-ranging%20presentation%20about%20the%20status%20of,is%20expected%20to%20begin%20%5Bin%5D%20summer%20of%202024.%E2%80%9D), then, in the summer of 2024, [the agency announced another postponement](https://mass.streetsblog.org/2024/06/14/mbta-delays-fall-river-new-bedford-rail-service-til-2025), to the spring of 2025.

### Recommended

[Rail](https://mass.streetsblog.org/category/rail)

[### A Rider’s Guide to the New Fall River/New Bedford Regional Rail Line](https://mass.streetsblog.org/2025/03/24/a-riders-guide-to-the-new-fall-river-new-bedford-regional-rail-line)

[Christian MilNeil](https://mass.streetsblog.org/author/christianmilneil)

March 24, 2025

[![Image 6](https://lede-admin.mass.streetsblog.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/49/2025/03/2025-03-04-fall-river-new-bedford-line-map_40c730-e1742830280833.png?resize=2880%2C1620)](https://mass.streetsblog.org/2025/03/24/a-riders-guide-to-the-new-fall-river-new-bedford-regional-rail-line)

However, there's been one silver lining to the delays. Under the T's initial service plans, the agency would have run 14 trains per weekday to New Bedford, plus 12 to the Fall River and Freetown branch.

[Under the actual operating schedule that begins today](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/media/route_pdfs/batch_7394/2025-03-24-cr-spring-summer-fall-river-new-bedford-line.pdf), the T is running 15 direct trains to and from Fall River, plus 17 round-trips to New Bedford.

Additionally, the T is planning a connecting shuttle service between East Taunton and Fall River or New Bedford, with cross-platform transfers at the East Taunton station, so that passengers in either city can get home even when a direct train isn't available.

Governor Healey and senior officials from her administration are also planning to celebrate the new transit line's grand opening this morning.

Governor Healey and General Manager Eng plan to ride [the northbound 10:38 a.m. train from Fall River to East Taunton](https://www.mbta.com/schedules/CR-NewBedford/timetable?date=2025-03-24&schedule_direction[direction_id]=1#direction-filter), where they'll meet Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll and MassDOT Secretary Secretary Monica Tibbits-Nutt, who plan to catch [the 10:43 a.m. train from New Bedford](https://www.mbta.com/schedules/CR-NewBedford/timetable?date=2025-03-24&schedule_direction[direction_id]=1#direction-filter).

At the new East Taunton station, the administration will host a celebratory press conference at 11:30 a.m.

_This story will be updated._

| | **South Coast Rail** is a project to expand the [MBTA Commuter Rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail "MBTA Commuter Rail") system into the [South Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_/(Massachusetts/) "South Coast (Massachusetts)") region of [Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts "Massachusetts"), United States. The first phase opened on March 24, 2025, becoming part of the [Fall River/New Bedford Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line "Fall River/New Bedford Line"). It extended service from [Middleborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough,_Massachusetts "Middleborough, Massachusetts") via [Taunton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton,_Massachusetts "Taunton, Massachusetts") with branches to [Fall River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River,_Massachusetts "Fall River, Massachusetts"), and [New Bedford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bedford,_Massachusetts "New Bedford, Massachusetts"). Six stations and two layover yards were constructed and 36.1 miles (58.1 km) of freight railroad track were rebuilt for passenger service. Previous passenger service to the South Coast ran over four different routes: via [Mansfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansfield,_Massachusetts "Mansfield, Massachusetts"), via [Stoughton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoughton,_Massachusetts "Stoughton, Massachusetts"), via [Randolph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randolph,_Massachusetts "Randolph, Massachusetts"), and via Middleborough. The first lines reached Taunton in 1836, New Bedford in 1840, and Fall River in 1846. The network of lines in southeastern Massachusetts was consolidated by 1888 under the [Old Colony Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad "Old Colony Railroad"), which was in turn acquired by the [New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York,_New_Haven_and_Hartford_Railroad "New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad") in 1893. Passenger service peaked in the early 20th century and declined thereafter, with the final service to the South Coast in 1958. The [Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Transportation_Authority "Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority") (MBTA) began planning the restoration of South Coast service in the 1980s. Feasibility studies were released in 1990 and 1995; the MBTA filed plans for a route using a new bypass near [Attleboro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attleboro,_Massachusetts "Attleboro, Massachusetts") in 1995. Environmental impact statements instead recommended a route via Stoughton, which required reactivating an abandoned section of rail line. Planning was suspended in 2002 due to increasing costs but resumed several years later. In 2010, the state purchased the rail lines from [CSX Transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CSX_Transportation "CSX Transportation"). Environmental impact statements in 2011 and 2013 again recommended the Stoughton route; state officials mandated that the service be electrified. In March 2017, the project was split into two phases due to high costs and long construction timelines. Phase 1 would provide interim diesel service to Fall River and New Bedford via Middleborough as an extension of the existing [Middleborough/Lakeville Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough/Lakeville_Line "Middleborough/Lakeville Line"). Phase 2 would complete the northern section of the project between Stoughton and Taunton and add electrification to the Phase 1 portion. Phase 1 construction began in 2019 with a projected cost of $1.047 billion and opened on March 24, 2025. Phase 2, which is not funded, would result in a total projected cost of $3.42 billion if built. [![Image 125: A high-level railway station platform with trains on both sides](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ae/Outbound_MBTA_New_Bedford_train_2021_and_Fall_River_train_1971_at_East_Taunton_March_2025_1.jpg/250px-Outbound_MBTA_New_Bedford_train_2021_and_Fall_River_train_1971_at_East_Taunton_March_2025_1.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Outbound_MBTA_New_Bedford_train_2021_and_Fall_River_train_1971_at_East_Taunton_March_2025_1.jpg) Two trains at [East Taunton station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Taunton_station "East Taunton station") The project, primarily located in the [South Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_/(Massachusetts/) "South Coast (Massachusetts)") region of Massachusetts, is split into two phases. Phase 1 opened on March 24, 2025, as part of the [Fall River/New Bedford Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line "Fall River/New Bedford Line"). It was an extension of the existing [Middleborough/Lakeville Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough/Lakeville_Line "Middleborough/Lakeville Line") using diesel-hauled trains. The Phase 1 routing splits from the [Middleborough Main Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough_Main_Line "Middleborough Main Line") in downtown [Middleborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough,_Massachusetts "Middleborough, Massachusetts"), with [Middleborough station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough_station "Middleborough station") replacing [Middleborough/Lakeville station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough/Lakeville_station "Middleborough/Lakeville station"). It runs west along the [Middleboro Secondary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleboro_Secondary "Middleboro Secondary") through [Lakeville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lakeville,_Massachusetts "Lakeville, Massachusetts") and [Taunton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton,_Massachusetts "Taunton, Massachusetts") to Cotley Junction, where it turns southeast onto the [New Bedford Main Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bedford_Secondary "New Bedford Secondary") and reaches [East Taunton station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Taunton_station "East Taunton station"). At [Myricks Junction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myricks,_Massachusetts "Myricks, Massachusetts") in [Berkley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkley,_Massachusetts "Berkley, Massachusetts") it splits into two southern branches. The Fall River Branch follows the [Fall River Secondary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River_Secondary "Fall River Secondary") southwest through [Freetown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freetown,_Massachusetts "Freetown, Massachusetts") and [Fall River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River,_Massachusetts "Fall River, Massachusetts"), with stops at [Freetown station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freetown_station "Freetown station") and [Fall River station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River_station "Fall River station"). The New Bedford Branch follows the New Bedford Main Line southeast through Lakeville, Freetown, and [New Bedford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bedford,_Massachusetts "New Bedford, Massachusetts"), with stops at [Church Street station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_Street_station_/(MBTA/) "Church Street station (MBTA)") and [New Bedford station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bedford_station "New Bedford station").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-2)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-dseir-1): 48 Phase 1 added passenger service to 36.1 miles (58.1 km) of track. The 7.1-mile (11.4 km) section of the Middleboro Secondary used for the project is single track with one siding. The 4.3 miles (6.9 km) of the New Bedford Main Line between Cotley Junction and Myricks Junction are double track, while the 14.0 miles (22.5 km) between Myricks Junction and New Bedford are a mix of single and double track. The 10.7 miles (17.2 km) of the Fall River Secondary are also a mixture.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-dseir-1): 52  [Positive train control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positive_train_control "Positive train control") was installed on the lines for the project.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-dseir-1): 54  Except for sidings and the Church Street–New Bedford section, the track was built to support passenger train speeds of 79 miles per hour (127 km/h).[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-dseir-1): 53  [Layover yards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Massachusetts_Bay_Transportation_Authority_yards "List of Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority yards") were built at Weaver's Cove in northern Fall River and Wamsutta near the New Bedford station.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-dseir-1): 4  The six new stations are [accessible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accessible "Accessible") with full-length high-level platforms.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-dseir-1): 56–58  Construction cost for Phase 1 was estimated as $1.047 billion in 2019 (equivalent to $1.26 billion in 2024).[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-spring2019-3) [![Image 126: A one-story Richardsonian Romanesque train station next to a disused track](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/ba/North_Easton_station_from_the_southwest%2C_June_2017.JPG/250px-North_Easton_station_from_the_southwest%2C_June_2017.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:North_Easton_station_from_the_southwest,_June_2017.JPG) The former station building at North Easton, proposed to be the site of Easton Village station Phase 2 ("full build"), which is proposed but not funded, would turn the South Coast lines into an extension of the Stoughton Branch of the [Providence/Stoughton Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Providence/Stoughton_Line "Providence/Stoughton Line"). From [Stoughton station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoughton_station "Stoughton station"), it would run south along the former [Dighton and Somerset Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dighton_and_Somerset_Railroad "Dighton and Somerset Railroad") through [Easton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easton,_Massachusetts "Easton, Massachusetts"), [Raynham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raynham,_Massachusetts "Raynham, Massachusetts"), and Taunton. At Weir Junction in Taunton, it would turn southeast onto the New Bedford Main Line, meeting the Phase 1 routing at Cotley Junction. New intermediate stops would be added at North Easton station, [Easton Village station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easton_Village_station "Easton Village station"), [Raynham Place station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raynham_Place_station "Raynham Place station"), and [Taunton station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_station_/(Old_Colony_Railroad/) "Taunton station (Old Colony Railroad)"). The Fall River Branch would also be extended south to a new [Battleship Cove station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battleship_Cove_station "Battleship Cove station"). The Stoughton Branch, the new segments, and the Phase 1 segments (except for the Middleboro Secondary) would be electrified.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-4) Total cost for the both phases was estimated as $3.4 billion in 2017 (equivalent to $4.1 billion in 2024).[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sharp-5) Unlike Phase 1, Phase 2 would involve reactivation of [previously abandoned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abandoned_railway#In_the_United_States "Abandoned railway") railroad right-of-way, as the portion between southern Stoughton and eastern Taunton was abandoned around the 1960s.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-fseir-6): 1–6 [\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-abandoned-7) In southern Easton and northern Raynham, the route passes through the [Hockomock Swamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hockomock_Swamp "Hockomock Swamp") on a low embankment, which is partially rewilded though used by pedestrians and [all-terrain vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-terrain_vehicle "All-terrain vehicle") riders. The swamp is a designated [Area of Critical Environmental Concern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area_of_Critical_Environmental_Concern_/(Massachusetts/) "Area of Critical Environmental Concern (Massachusetts)") and houses several endangered species including the [blue-spotted salamander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue-spotted_salamander "Blue-spotted salamander").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-app417a-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-10) An 8,500-foot (2,600 m) trestle atop the embankment is proposed to allow animals to pass under the tracks and limit the disturbance to the existing ground. The trestle would use concrete box girders on piles spaced at 50 feet (15 m), with a maintenance siding in the middle.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-app32c-11)[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-13) [![Image 127: A postcard of a railway station with an Egyptian Revival style facade](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/90/New_Bedford_old_station_postcard.jpg/250px-New_Bedford_old_station_postcard.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:New_Bedford_old_station_postcard.jpg) The first station in New Bedford Previous passenger service to the South Coast ran over four different routes: via [Mansfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansfield,_Massachusetts "Mansfield, Massachusetts"), via [Stoughton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoughton,_Massachusetts "Stoughton, Massachusetts"), via [Randolph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randolph,_Massachusetts "Randolph, Massachusetts"), and via [Middleborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough,_Massachusetts "Middleborough, Massachusetts"). The first rail line to reach the area was the [Taunton Branch Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Branch_Railroad "Taunton Branch Railroad"), which connected with the [Boston and Providence Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_and_Providence_Railroad "Boston and Providence Railroad") (B&P) at Mansfield. It opened to [Taunton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton,_Massachusetts "Taunton, Massachusetts") in August 1836; a closely affiliated extension, the [New Bedford and Taunton Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bedford_and_Taunton_Railroad "New Bedford and Taunton Railroad"), opened to New Bedford in July 1840.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sne-14): 39–398  The [Middleborough and Taunton Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough_and_Taunton_Railroad "Middleborough and Taunton Railroad") opened in July 1856; it connected with the New Bedford and Taunton at Cotley Junction south of Taunton.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sne-14): 398 The first segment of what would become the [Fall River Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River_Railroad_/(1846/) "Fall River Railroad (1846)") opened from [Myricks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myricks,_Massachusetts "Myricks, Massachusetts") (on the New Bedford and Taunton) to Fall River on June 9, 1845.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-1911report-15)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-16) The rest of the line opened in 1846 from Myricks through Middleborough to [South Braintree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braintree_station_/(MBTA/)#History "Braintree station (MBTA)") on the [Old Colony Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#Old_Colony_Railroad_\(1844%E2%80%931854\) "Old Colony Railroad"), creating a second route from Fall River to Boston. The next year, owner [Richard Borden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Borden "Richard Borden") founded the [Fall River Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River_Line "Fall River Line"), which operated New York–Fall River steamship service. It connected with the "Boat Train" on the Fall River Railroad to provide New York–Boston through service.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sne-14): 403  The Old Colony Railroad and the Fall River Railroad merged in 1854 as the [Old Colony and Fall River Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_and_Fall_River_Railroad "Old Colony and Fall River Railroad"). It merged with the [Newport and Fall River Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_and_Fall_River_Railroad "Newport and Fall River Railroad") in 1863 to become the [Old Colony and Newport Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_and_Newport_Railway "Old Colony and Newport Railway"), then with the [Cape Cod Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod_Railroad "Cape Cod Railroad") in 1872 to become the [Old Colony Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad "Old Colony Railroad").[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 95 The [Stoughton Branch Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoughton_Branch_Railroad "Stoughton Branch Railroad") opened in April 1845 from Stoughton to [Canton Junction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canton_Junction_station "Canton Junction station") on the B&P.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sne-14): 181  An extension, the [Easton Branch Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Easton_Branch_Railroad&action=edit&redlink=1 "Easton Branch Railroad (page does not exist)"), opened to [North Easton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Easton,_Massachusetts "North Easton, Massachusetts") on May 16, 1855.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 29  In 1863, the [Dighton and Somerset Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dighton_and_Somerset_Railroad "Dighton and Somerset Railroad") began construction on a line between Somerset Junction (north of Fall River) and [Braintree Highlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braintree,_Massachusetts "Braintree, Massachusetts") – both on the Old Colony and Newport – via Taunton, North Easton, and Randolph. The Old Colony and Newport purchased the potential competitor in 1865 and opened it on September 24, 1866.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-secondsection-18): 11 [\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sne-14): 393  It used the Easton Branch Railroad between North Easton and Stoughton Junction (south of Stoughton); passenger service ended between Stoughton and Stoughton Junction. The new route via Randolph was shorter than the Middleborough and Mansfield routes; it became the Old Colony's primary Fall River–Boston routing.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sne-14): 394 [![Image 128: See caption.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/OC1893.jpg/250px-OC1893.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:OC1893.jpg) [Old Colony Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad "Old Colony Railroad") network in 1893 The Taunton Branch Railroad opened a branch from Attleboro Junction (west of Taunton) to [Attleboro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attleboro,_Massachusetts "Attleboro, Massachusetts") in 1871. The company merged with the New Bedford and Taunton in 1874 as the [New Bedford Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bedford_Railroad "New Bedford Railroad").[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sne-14): 398  The Old Colony acquired the Middleborough and Taunton Railroad in 1874 and a successor of the New Bedford Railroad in 1879.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sne-14): 399  Around 1882, the Old Colony opened the [Whittenton Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whittenton_Branch "Whittenton Branch") between Whittenton Junction (near Attleboro Junction) and [Raynham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raynham,_Massachusetts "Raynham, Massachusetts"). It allowed trains on the Dighton and Somerset to serve [Taunton Central station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_station_/(Amtrak/) "Taunton station (Amtrak)") rather than [Dean Street station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_station_/(Old_Colony_Railroad/) "Taunton station (Old Colony Railroad)"), thus consolidating Taunton's passenger services at a single station.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sne-14): 394 The Old Colony acquired the B&P in 1888, consolidating all the railways in southeastern Massachusetts under a single owner. The company expanded Mansfield–New Bedford service and routed some Fall River and New Bedford trains via Stoughton at times.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 31  The [New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York,_New_Haven_and_Hartford_Railroad "New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad") (New Haven) leased the Old Colony in 1893.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sne-14): 379  By 1898, daily South Coast service via Mansfield included six Taunton–Boston round trips and one New Bedford–Boston round trip plus nine New Bedford–Mansfield round trips that connected with Boston trains at Mansfield. Service via Randolph included one Taunton–Boston round trip and four [Newport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport,_Rhode_Island "Newport, Rhode Island")–Fall River–Boston round trips. There were three Fall River–Boston round trips via Middleborough.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 34 The opening of [South Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Station "South Station") in 1898 allowed increases in through service; by 1906; eleven of the fourteen daily New Bedford–Mansfield round trips ran to and from Boston.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 34  Service timed for Boston commuting had been available from Taunton and New Bedford via Mansfield since around 1885.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 31  Fall River never had a strong commuter market to Boston; commuter service via Middleborough was available for several years starting in 1915.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 95 [\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-secondsection-18): 30  Commuter service via Randolph never ran further south than North Easton.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 95 Cutbacks to service began during World War I and continued thereafter. Service between Mansfield and New Bedford was reduced sharply to five daily round trips, and Fall River service via Middleborough dwindled.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 34 [\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sne-14): 403  The New Haven resumed running South Coast trains via Stoughton during and after the war.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 34  Use of the Randolph route ended around 1924.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sne-14): 394  By 1927, all service to New Bedford and Fall River ran via Stoughton, save for a single Fall River round trip that ran via Middleborough until 1931.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 34, 96  Service on the southern part of the Dighton and Somerset ended in 1932, with Fall River service routed via Myricks thereafter.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sne-14): 395 South Coast service was rerouted via Mansfield in 1937 during the early stages of the [88 stations case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/88_stations_case "88 stations case"), which also brought the end of service south of Fall River in 1938.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 34  Fall River service was reduced to Taunton shuttles during World War II. New Bedford service was reduced to three round trips in March 1949, and the Fall River shuttles were discontinued that September. Most New Bedford service was routed via Stoughton in 1950; both routes were used for several years.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 35  Fall River shuttles resumed in June 1952.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-19)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 35 All service was routed via Stoughton in 1955 when a grade separation project at Mansfield cut the branch line. By that time there were three New Bedford–Boston round trips – one with a Fall River shuttle – and one Fall River–Boston trip.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 36  That remaining service ended on September 5, 1958, as the New Haven cut its unprofitable Old Colony Division; the remaining passenger service on the division ended the next year.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 36, 96  Freight service to the South Coast continued, though the remainder of the Dighton and Somerset was abandoned in the 1960s and 1970s.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-abandoned-7) The New Haven merged in late 1968 into [Penn Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penn_Central "Penn Central"), which merged into [Conrail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conrail "Conrail") in 1976. Passenger service continued on the ex-B&P, including the Stoughton Branch, eventually becoming the [Providence/Stoughton Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Providence/Stoughton_Line "Providence/Stoughton Line").[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sne-14): 19 South Coast Rail planning ------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=South_Coast_Rail&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: South Coast Rail planning")\] ### Restoration planning (1980s–2003) \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=South_Coast_Rail&action=edit§ion=9 "Edit section: Restoration planning (1980s–2003)")\] The [Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Transportation_Authority "Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority") (MBTA) was formed in 1964 to subsidize suburban rail service and build rapid transit extensions.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17) The MBTA purchased the Old Colony mainline between Boston and Braintree in 1965 for the construction of the Braintree Branch of the [Red Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Line_/(MBTA/) "Red Line (MBTA)").[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-20) Contraction of the New Haven's Boston commuter service largely ended after 1967; expansion of service frequency and area began in the late 1970s.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17) In 1970, following [revolts against freeways in the urban core](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highway_revolts_in_the_United_States#Massachusetts "Highway revolts in the United States"), Massachusetts governor [Francis Sargent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Sargent "Francis Sargent") placed a moratorium on new highway construction inside the [Route 128 beltway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Route_128 "Massachusetts Route 128"). The resulting cancellation of the [Southwest Expressway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwest_Corridor_/(Massachusetts/)#Highway_proposal "Southwest Corridor (Massachusetts)") by the [Boston Transportation Planning Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Transportation_Planning_Review "Boston Transportation Planning Review") meant the already-overcrowded [Southeast Expressway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Expressway_/(Massachusetts/) "Southeast Expressway (Massachusetts)") would continue to be the only highway into Boston from the south.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-problem3-21): 36 [\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 16  The MBTA purchased many of the Penn Central suburban lines in January 1973. These included the ex-B&P lines, the disused line from Stoughton to Whittenton Junction via Raynham, and part of the Middleborough Main Line.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-22)[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-23)[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-24) In the 1980s, the restoration of the lines to New Bedford and Fall River was proposed. Since the routes via Mansfield and Randolph and the Middleborough–Myricks segment of the Middleborough route were abandoned and built over, three possible routes to the South Coast were placed under consideration: the Stoughton route, a route following the Northeast Corridor to near [Attleboro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attleboro_station_/(Massachusetts/) "Attleboro station (Massachusetts)") and then branching onto the [Attleboro Secondary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attleboro_Secondary "Attleboro Secondary"), and a route following the [Middleborough Main Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough_Main_Line "Middleborough Main Line") to Middleborough then the [Middleboro Secondary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleboro_Secondary "Middleboro Secondary") westwards. All three routes used the same lines from Taunton south to Fall River and New Bedford. By 1988, the MBTA was tentatively planning to extend service to Taunton via Stoughton.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-25) The first major study, completed in January 1990, concluded that the Stoughton Branch was the most viable route. The study was criticized for not considering other alternatives, including express buses.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-1995report-26): 1–5  A May 1991 bond bill included $3 million (equivalent to $6 million in 2024) for planning the extension.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-timeline-27)[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-28) In 1991, the state agreed to build a set of transit projects as part of an agreement with the [Conservation Law Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservation_Law_Foundation "Conservation Law Foundation") (CLF), which had threatened a lawsuit over auto emissions from the Central Artery/Tunnel Project ([Big Dig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Dig "Big Dig")). Among these projects was the "Old Colony Commuter Rail Line Extension", to be complete by the end of 1996.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-1991agreement-29)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-30)[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-31) This included the [Middleborough/Lakeville Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough/Lakeville_Line "Middleborough/Lakeville Line") and [Plymouth/Kingston Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plymouth/Kingston_Line "Plymouth/Kingston Line"), which opened in 1997, plus the 2007-opened [Greenbush Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenbush_Line "Greenbush Line").[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-netransit-32) Planning for service to the South Coast continued. The March 1995 _Expanded Feasibility Study_ analyzed routes absent from the 1990 report. The 1965–1980 construction of the Braintree Branch had only left space for a single track (intended for freight use) on the Old Colony mainline through parts of [Dorchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorchester,_Boston "Dorchester, Boston") and [Quincy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincy,_Massachusetts "Quincy, Massachusetts").[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-problem3-21): 36 [\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-clarke-33): i, 1, 4  This limited the capacity required for reaching the South Coast via Middleborough: service could be operated to one of Fall River and New Bedford, but not both.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-1995report-26): ii  The report concluded that both the Stoughton and Attleboro routes would be viable and that a partial [Stoughton Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoughton_Branch "Stoughton Branch") extension to [North Easton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Easton "North Easton") would be most cost-effective.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-1995report-26): ii [![Image 129: See caption.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/Attleboro_Bypass_proposal_map.svg/250px-Attleboro_Bypass_proposal_map.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Attleboro_Bypass_proposal_map.svg) Map of the Attleboro Bypass proposal In September 1995, the MBTA filed plans with the [Environmental Protection Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Environmental_Protection_Agency "United States Environmental Protection Agency") (EPA) for service via the Attleboro route. It was to include a 3-mile (4.8 km) 'Attleboro Bypass' on new right-of-way connecting the [Northeast Corridor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeast_Corridor "Northeast Corridor") to the Attleboro Secondary northeast of downtown Attleboro. The project was to be completed in 2000 at a cost of $156 million (equivalent to $292 million in 2024).[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-34) In August 1996, Governor [Bill Weld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Weld "Bill Weld") signed a bill giving $136 million (equivalent to $250 million in 2024) to commuter rail expansion, while the state legislature directed the MBTA to further study alternatives.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-srpedd-35) The 1997 _Expanded Alternatives Analysis_ showed vastly increased costs — $407 million (equivalent to $737 million in 2024) via Attleboro, $410 million ($742 million) via Stoughton, or $436 million ($789 million) via Middleborough. Service via Middleborough would also require double-tracking on the Old Colony mainline at additional cost. The report recommended the Stoughton route as the most cost-effective due to its high ridership.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-timeline-27)[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-1997report-36) A groundbreaking ceremony was held in October 1998 after a contract for bridge work in Fall River and New Bedford was awarded that month.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-timeline-27)[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-37) Based on an analysis of South Station operations, the July 1999 _Draft Environmental Impact Report_ concluded that the Stoughton route was the only viable route. It projected 4,325 daily riders with 20 trains per day to each of Fall River and New Bedford.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-38)[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-39) In January 2000, following then-governor [Paul Cellucci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Cellucci "Paul Cellucci")'s reapproval, the state reported that construction would begin in late 2002 and last until 2004.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-timeline-27) The Draft Environmental Statement certificate was received in November 2000; the EPA confirmed that Stoughton was the only practical route but required a Final Environmental Impact Statement (FEIS).[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-srpedd-35) The FEIS was released in April 2002 and approved in August. The state's approval required the Southeastern Regional Planning and Economic Development District (SRPEDD) to establish a Growth Task Force. In July 2002, the MBTA revised the project cost to $600 million (equivalent to $997 million in 2024) with an opening date of 2007.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-timeline-27)[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-srpedd-35) Due to the increasing costs, the MBTA suspended the Growth Task Force and stopped project planning in November 2002; the environmental approval process was stopped in May 2003.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-srpedd-35) ### Restoration planning (2005–2014) \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=South_Coast_Rail&action=edit§ion=10 "Edit section: Restoration planning (2005–2014)")\] The SRPEDD restarted the Growth Task Force in October 2004 even though the MBTA was still conducting its review of the project.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-srpedd-35) In March 2005, Governor [Mitt Romney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitt_Romney "Mitt Romney") allowed the project to proceed and allocated $670 million (equivalent to $1 billion in 2024) for the project, which was then projected to open between 2011 and 2013. The Chief of Commonwealth Development stated in June 2005 that the cost could be as high as $1 billion (equivalent to $1.5 billion in 2024).[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-timeline-27) In April 2007, the Massachusetts Executive Office of Transportation released _South Coast Rail: A Plan For Action_, which restarted the planning process from the beginning. The plan estimated project costs at $1.435 billion (equivalent to $2 billion in 2024), including $163 million ($237 million) for procuring additional rolling stock and $31.4 million ($46 million) for expanding [South Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Station "South Station"), with opening in December 2016.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-40) The Phase 1 "Vanasse Hangen Brustlin, Inc.") and [HNTB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HNTB "HNTB") for "program management, early design development, and environmental permitting".[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-60) ### Project changes (2016–2021) \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=South_Coast_Rail&action=edit§ion=11 "Edit section: Project changes (2016–2021)")\] In June 2016, the MBTA announced that the project cost had been revised to $3.42 billion (equivalent to $4 billion in 2024), with completion not expected until 2030. Some local and regional officials objected to that plan, as it would have reduced service to Middleborough/Lakeville station and potentially interfered with Plymouth/Kingston Line and Greenbush Line service.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-june2016-61)[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-62) Design for the Stoughton route was 15% complete by that time.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-63) In March 2017, the state announced a revised plan intended to provide service sooner than 2030.
