The New Bedford mayor and transit advocates were critical of the longer travel times of the Middleborough routing, and the Taunton mayor was critical of Phase 1 lacking the [downtown Taunton station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_station_/(Old_Colony_Railroad/) "Taunton station (Old Colony Railroad)") of the previous plan.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sharp-5)[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-66) Stoughton, Easton, and Raynham officials continued their previous opposition to South Coast Rail.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sharp-5) The _Draft Supplemental Environmental Impact Report_ (DSEIR) was released in January 2018. Abandoned railbed along the Phase 2 route in Raynham The portion of the route between Stoughton and Taunton, proposed for construction in Phase 2, has proved the most controversial part of the project. While the cities of Taunton, Fall River, and New Bedford pushed for the project, the towns of [Raynham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raynham,_Massachusetts "Raynham, Massachusetts") and [Easton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easton,_Massachusetts "Easton, Massachusetts") objected to the Stoughton route beginning in the 1990s, citing concerns about pollution, traffic, and grade crossing safety. The two towns began legal action opposing the project in 1997; [Stoughton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoughton,_Massachusetts "Stoughton, Massachusetts") joined in 2001. Their legal fight focused on potential impacts to the [Hockomock Swamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hockomock_Swamp "Hockomock Swamp").[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-116) In his 2002 approval of the Final Environmental Impact Report, Secretary of Environmental Affairs [Robert Durand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Durand "Robert Durand") mandated the construction of [a trestle through the swamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#Phase_2) to reduce impacts.[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-117) Later planning included the trestle plan.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-pineswamp-12): 4 In 2007, voters in Raynham elected to seek mitigation for impacts rather than continue litigation. Easton voters made the same choice in 2008.[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-directions-118)[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-119) In 2009, Stoughton officials indicated that they would seek for a tunnel to be built through the downtown area — as was done in [Hingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hingham,_Massachusetts "Hingham, Massachusetts") on the [Greenbush Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenbush_Line "Greenbush Line") — with [Stoughton station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoughton_station "Stoughton station") moved underground.[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-120)[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-121) A town committee found that the state was unlikely to fund such a plan.[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-directions-118) In 2014, Raynham officials expressed interest in lowering tracks under [Route 138](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Route_138 "Massachusetts Route 138") to prevent traffic impacts.[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-122) When plans for the phased approach were announced in 2017, Stoughton, Easton, and Raynham officials continued their previous opposition to the project.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sharp-5)[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-:9-123) Whether Phase 2 of the project will ever be built is unclear.[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-finished-124)[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-125) By mid-2024, MassDOT no longer indicated that it would be built by 2030.[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-finished-124) No funding for Phase 2 was included in the MBTA's FY 2026–2030 capital investment plan in 2025.[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-126)[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-127)[\[125\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-128) Corridor map for the South Coast Rail project showing the project's phasing plan. Phase 1 will extend the existing


Middleborough/Lakeville Commuter Rail Line to provide service to Taunton, New Bedford and Fall River. The Phase 1 route begins at


South Station in Boston and continues on the existing Middleborough Main Line to Pilgrim Junction, then follows the Middleborough


Secondary to Cotley Junction. The route then continues south and splits into two legs: one leg bound for Fall River following the Fall


River Secondary and one leg bound for New Bedford following the New Bedford Main Line. Existing stations and layovers for Phase 1


include South Station, Holbrook/Randolph, Montello, Brockton, Campello, Bridgewater, Middleborough/Lakeville, and Middleborough


Layover. Phase 1 includes four new stations: East Taunton, Fall River Depot, King's Highway, and Whale's Tooth; a potential new


Middleborough station; and two new layover facilities (Weaver's Cove and Wamsutta).


Phase 2 follows the Northeast Corridor from Boston to Canton Junction, then follows the Stoughton Line to Cotley Junction. Existing


stations include South Station, Back Bay, Ruggles, Forest Hills, Readville, Route 128, and Canton Junction. Reconstructed stations


include Canton Center and Stoughton stations. New stations for phase 2 include: North Easton, Easton Village, Raynham Place,


Taunton, Freetown, and Battleship Cove.

![Image 1: A bird's eye view of the New Bedford station on the MBTA's South Coast Rail line.](https://i0.wp.com/newspack-thepublicsradio.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/2024/04/1023_newbed-rail-03.jpeg?fit=1200%2C900&ssl=1)

South Coast Rail will stop in New Bedford at a station near the waterfront, about a mile from the city’s downtown. Credit: Robbin Lubbock / WBUR

MBTA officials have pushed the target opening date for South Coast Rail back to May 2025, delaying the long-awaited restoration of train service to Fall River, New Bedford and Taunton by another year.

MBTA General Manager Phillip Eng, the agency’s top official, delivered the news personally at a pair of public meetings in Fall River and New Bedford Thursday night, which his staff had rushed to publicize with only a day’s notice.

Eng, who was hired last year, attributed the project’s latest delay to a previous lack of understanding among MBTA officials about how long safety testing takes on a new rail line. Eng [parted ways with South Coast Rail’s top project manager](https://thepublicsradio.org/transportation/south-coast-rail-delayed-again-as-mbta-parts-ways-with-projects-top-manager/), Jennifer Tabakin, earlier this year.

Eng said the project’s new leader, Karen Anton, needed several months to re-evaluate where South Coast Rail stands and publicize a more realistic completion date. In her own remarks, Anton said she’s led several rail projects through the federal safety testing regimen known as the New Starts Process, which she projected South Coast Rail will begin in February 2025.

“And when I checked, I didn’t see that anybody had really spent a lot of time talking to anybody about the New Starts Process,” Anton said, “which is pretty incredible because it’s a pretty important process.”

The news of another delay for South Coast Rail felt like a sore subject for many in attendance Thursday. Ken Fiola, an economic development consultant and business leader in Fall River, said he’s been watching deadlines for the rail project slip since the 1990s.

The MBTA more recently promised to complete South Coast Rail by summer 2023. The agency pushed that deadline back to summer 2024, before walking it back again at Thursday’s meeting by almost an entire year.

“If nothing else, I think the MBTA owes this region — and this city, and the residents of this area — an apology,” Fiola said during a public comment period. “An apology for misleading the entire region with false promises and deadlines.”

“And I understand that may not have occurred under your watch,” Fiola continued, addressing Eng, “but I really have to question the transparency of the process to date and the information that has been disseminated today.”

Eng did not apologize, but promised that “we are going to do everything we can to beat that May date.”

![Image 2: MBTA General Manager Phillip Eng speaks with reporters.](https://i0.wp.com/newspack-thepublicsradio.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/2024/06/Phillip-Eng-1024x768.jpg?resize=780%2C585&ssl=1)

MBTA General Manager Phillip Eng, flanked by Chief Operating Officer Ryan Coholan and Assistant General Manager Sam Zhou, visited Fall River in person to deliver the news of South Coast Rail’s delay. Credit: Ben Berke / The Public's Radio

Despite the significant delay, Eng said in an interview that the project remains on budget at about $1 billion.

The train line itself [follows a circuitous route to Boston’s South Station](https://thepublicsradio.org/article/in-bid-for-service-sooner-south-coast-rail-takes-the-long-way-to-boston/) that MBTA officials estimate will take about 90 minutes, regardless of whether a passenger boards in Fall River or New Bedford. The line follows a reconstructed freight railroad before linking into the pre-existing Middleboro/Lakeville Commuter Rail branch, which then converges onto a congested trunk line with other Boston-bound trains that will significantly limit the frequency of service to the South Coast.

The challenging logistics of that journey have prevented MBTA officials from offering a definitive answer as to whether South Coast Rail will run on the weekends.

“We believe that we’ll be able to run some service,” Eng said about weekends. “What we need to do is to be able to work through those different logistics, and what we don’t want to do is lead the public astray.”

When South Coast Rail opens, it will restore passenger train service to Fall River, New Bedford and Taunton for the first time since the 1950s, giving people a long-awaited alternative to driving on Massachusetts’ congested highways.

Eng’s team announced for the first time on Thursday how much fares on the new line will cost. A one-way ticket from New Bedford or Fall River to Boston is priced at $12.25. People with lower incomes can apply to qualify for a reduced $6 fare.

[![Image 3: Avatar photo](https://thepublicsradio.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/benberkeheadshotbw-80x80.jpg)](https://thepublicsradio.org/author/ben-berke/)

Based in New Bedford, Ben staffs our South Coast Bureau desk. He covers anything that happens in Fall River, New Bedford, and the surrounding towns, as long as it's a good story. His assignments have taken...

The Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA) has announced that the South Coast Rail passenger service will commence on Monday 24 March 2025, pending final approval from the Federal Railroad Administration (FRA).

This marks the return of passenger rail service to Taunton, Freetown, New Bedford, Middleboro, and Fall River for the first time in 65 years.

![Image 1: New Bedford station](https://railway-news.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/2024-04-SCR-New-Bedford-Renovated-Station-Platform-scaled.jpg)

New Bedford station

© MBTA

The South Coast Rail project extends service on the current Middleborough/Lakeville Line, which will be renamed the Fall River/New Bedford Line when service begins.

The South Coast Rail service will include:

*   15 weekday trips on the Fall River Line and 17 weekday trips on the New Bedford Line
*   32 total weekday trips between South Station and East Taunton
*   26 weekend trips between South Station and East Taunton

Trains will run every 70 minutes on weekdays and every two hours on weekends. Late-night service will see the final train from Boston departing just before midnight.

> The people of Taunton, Freetown, New Bedford, Middleboro and Fall River have been waiting for passenger rail service for far too long. General Manager Eng and his team aren’t kicking the can down the road – they're delivering. We’re thrilled to soon be launching South Coast Rail service, which will make it easier for South Coast residents to get around the state, reduce congestion and spur economic development.

South Coast Rail’s six new stations—Middleborough, East Taunton, Freetown, Fall River Depot, Church Street, and New Bedford—were completed by September 2024 and are fully accessible.

Safety testing for Automatic Train Control (ATC) was completed in July 2024, with dispatch responsibilities transferred to Keolis. More than 800 Positive Train Control (PTC) functions have been tested, with final operations handed over to Keolis in January 2025.

Qualification runs for operator training and route familiarisation are currently underway, with demonstration service planned for early March. Additional signage, station posters, route maps, and street signs will be installed in the coming weeks as part of the final preparation for service commencement.

> MBTA General Manager and CEO Phillip Eng said:Delivering new rail service to the communities as part of South Coast Rail is another example of our workforce fulfilling commitments made to the public. The MBTA is proud to be in this position working collaboratively with the Federal Railroad Administration as we now seek their approval to begin passenger train service at the end of March ahead of our May target. This will allow communities in Boston, southeastern Massachusetts, and many in between to connect by train for the first time in decades.

South Coast Rail fares will be set at Zone 8 pricing, meaning a full fare of 12.25 USD and a reduced fare of 6 USD.

1.content:
![Image 1: Two trains pulled into the platforms at East Taunton Commuter Rail station](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/styles/max_2600x2600/public/media/2025-04/2025-03-24-south-coast-rail-east-taunton-opening.jpg?itok=BPrgcX6B)

The East Taunton station platform on the first day of Fall River/New Bedford Line service (March 24, 2025)

About This Project
------------------

![Image 2: Newly renovated New Bedford station with station sign and platform with yellow tactile surface indicator ](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/styles/max_2600x2600/public/media/2024-06/2024-04-SCR-New-Bedford-Renovated-Station-Platform.jpg?itok=F511KnUe)

New Bedford station platform (April 2024)

The [South Coast Rail project](https://www.mass.gov/south-coast-rail) offers a reliable transit connection between southeastern Massachusetts and Boston. Riders can take a one-seat trip for the first time since the late 1950s.

The project creates connections between Boston and the communities of Taunton, New Bedford, and Fall River, the only three major cities within 50 miles of Boston that previously didn’t have Commuter Rail access.

[Learn more about the South Coast Rail Program](https://www.mass.gov/service-details/about-the-south-coast-rail-project)

Building a Better T
-------------------

As part of our $9.6 billion, [5-year capital investment plan](https://www.mbta.com/cip), we're renovating stations, modernizing fare collection systems, upgrading services for our buses, subways, and ferries, and improving the accessibility of the entire system.

[Learn more](https://www.mbta.com/projects)

Schedules
---------

On weekdays, trains run every 70 minutes. There are 32 direct trips to or from [South Station](https://www.mbta.com/stops/place-sstat) including:

*   15 trips between South Station and Fall River
*   17 trips between South Station and New Bedford

On weekends, there are 26 total trips with trains running every two hours.

[View the Fall River/New Bedford Line schedule](https://www.mbta.com/schedules/CR-NewBedford/timetable)

[Check alerts for the Fall River/New Bedford Line](https://www.mbta.com/schedules/CR-NewBedford/alerts)

### Scheduled Transfers at East Taunton Station

In addition to the 32 direct trips to or from South Station on weekdays, we operate connecting trains between:

*   Fall River Depot and East Taunton station
*   New Bedford station and East Taunton station

Riders can transfer between connecting trains and direct trains at East Taunton station where the Fall River and New Bedford branches meet. This means riders on both branches can access more trips to or from South Station throughout the weekday.

For example, riders going between New Bedford and South Station can get to their destination even if the next direct trip is between Fall River and South Station:

1.  At New Bedford station, board the connecting train going to East Taunton station.
2.  At East Taunton station, exit the connecting train to make a transfer.
3.  Board the direct train that came from Fall River Depot and is continuing to South Station.

1.  At South Station, board the direct train going to Fall River Depot.
2.  At East Taunton station, exit the direct train to make a transfer.
3.  Board the connecting train going to New Bedford station.

We've coordinated train schedules to ensure that riders always have enough time to transfer at East Taunton.

* * *

Safety First Program
--------------------

**Safety First** is a program that educates people on how to stay safe around train tracks. Our goal is to bring an understanding of safety rules to all residents in every southeastern Massachusetts city and town.

Through presentations, brochures, videos, meetings, and conversations, you’ll learn safety basics. You can watch and share our [Safety Video Series](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLpgUaADAtNfuJKpPGysCprwkepiOC-DBZ) developed for children, teens, and the general public to learn about the importance of safety for everyone throughout the region.

Watch our safety videos, and please think **Safety First**.

To request rail safety education or materials, call Customer Support at [617-222-3200](tel:617-222-3200) or fill out our [Customer Support form](https://www.mbta.com/customer-support).

[Download a Safety First fact sheet](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/2023-12-safety-first-fact-sheet.pdf) (PDF, 926 KB)

[### Commuter Rail Safety](https://www.mbta.com/safety/commuter-rail-safety)![Image 3: Bi-level Commuter Rail coaches at the newly-completed Freetown Station](https://live-mbta.pantheonsite.io/sites/default/files/styles/teaser/public/media/2023-03/2023-3-3-cr-scr-freetown-ribbon-cutting-double-car-view.jpg?itok=9iFomq_d)

Commuter Rail safety is important to the MBTA. We aim to educate our riders and community members about Commuter Rail safety to prevent any accidents or close calls.

[Learn more](https://www.mbta.com/safety/commuter-rail-safety)

Construction Timeline
---------------------

South Coast Rail is being built in phases:

*   **Phase 1:** Extended the former Middleborough/Lakeville Line, now named the Fall River/New Bedford Line. Service on the [Fall River/New Bedford Line](https://www.mbta.com/schedules/CR-NewBedford/timetable) started March 24, 2025.
*   **Full Build:** Extends the Stoughton Line south to connect more communities to the Fall River/New Bedford Line.

Phase 1 broke ground in July 2019, with major construction beginning in 2020. After we completed construction of stations, tracks, and signals, we also conducted rigorous testing to meet safety certifications and qualifications that precede passenger service.

Construction was divided into two contracts, with early action work preceding both:

*   Construction of the Fall River Secondary Line, which will connect Fall River to Boston
*   Construction of the New Bedford Main Line, the Middleborough Secondary Line, and the signal system for the entire Phase 1 corridor, which will connect Taunton, New Bedford, and Fall River to Boston

[See a map of the Phase 1 corridor](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/2024-12-18-south-coast-rail-phase-1-corridor-map-updated.pdf) (PDF, 9.1 MB)

![Image 4: A crew works on culvert installation in Lakeville as part of the South Coast Rail project (May 2020)](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/styles/max_650x650/public/media/2020-05/SCR_Culvert_Installation2020.jpg?itok=7KdZdwqv)

A crew replaces rail above a completed culvert installation in Lakeville as part of the South Coast Rail project (May 2020)

Our crews completed early action work in fall 2020 in preparation for Phase 1 construction:

*   Replaced four railroad bridges
*   Installed 46 culverts as part of the drainage system
*   Ordered and stored long-lead special track materials in advance to reduce construction delays
*   Constructed five wetland mitigation areas and began monitoring their success

[Learn more about early action work](https://www.mass.gov/lists/south-coast-rail-documents-and-meeting-materials#spring-2019-fact-sheet-)

![Image 5: 16 bi-level coaches, like the one pictured here, will be put into service as part of the South Coast Rail project ](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/styles/max_650x650/public/media/2020-05/SCR_Bi-levelCoach.jpg?itok=-3Jgz3cU)

16 bi-level coaches, like the one pictured here, will be put into service during Phase 1 of the South Coast Rail project

In October 2019, the Fiscal and Management Control Board (FMCB) [approved the purchase of 16 bi-level coaches](https://www.mbta.com/news/2019-09-23/fmcb-approves-the-procurement-80-new-commuter-rail-bi-level-coaches) to meet the needs of the South Coast Rail project. The refurbishment of two locomotives required for South Coast Rail service is also complete. As of summer 2023, these vehicles are part of the state's commuter rail system inventory.

*   ![Image 6: Newly completed Freetown Station platform](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/styles/max_650x650/public/media/2023-03/2023-3-3-cr-scr-freetown-ribbon-cutting-platform-view.jpg?itok=rACkugcF)
    
    The Completed Freetown Station during the ribbon-cutting event celebrating the substantial completion of the Fall River Secondary Line contract (December 2022)
    
*   The Fall River Secondary Line extends to Fall River through Freetown and Taunton, providing direct service between Fall River and Boston. This new Commuter Rail line includes two stations in Freetown and Fall River, and a layover facility at Weaver’s Cove in Fall River. We completed construction at the end of 2024.

**Completed Work**

Crews reconstructed 12.1 miles of the Fall River Secondary Line, which was previously a freight line, to lift speed restrictions and allow for Commuter Rail service. Work also included tree clearing, erosion control, and survey work along the tracks. The tracks were reconstructed, resulting in improved freight service in the region.

Construction included the following:

*   Nine rail bridges
*   10 new grade crossings and four interlockings
*   Two new stations and a layover facility for storing trains overnight

Trains on the completed Fall River Secondary Line travel through Berkley, Freetown, and Fall River.

[See a map of the Fall River Secondary Line](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/2020-05/SCR_FRS_Map.pdf)

![Image 7: view of rail layover yard with blue sky](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/styles/max_650x650/public/media/2025-01/2024-09-10-scr-wamsutta-layover-yard.jpeg?itok=BrdJ5T4o)

Wamsutta layover yard (September 2024)

The Middleborough Secondary Line extends from Middleborough through Taunton and into New Bedford to provide direct service between New Bedford and Boston.

The new Commuter Rail line includes four stations and a layover facility adjacent to the existing one in Wamsutta.

We completed construction for the Middleborough Secondary and New Bedford Main lines in fall 2024. We completed construction for the pedestrian bridge at [New Bedford](https://www.mbta.com/stops/place-NBM-0546) station in spring 2025.

**Completed Work**

Crews reconstructed 24.1 miles of Middleborough Secondary and the New Bedford Main lines, which are currently active freight lines, to lift speed restrictions and allow for Commuter Rail service. The right-of-way (ROW) was also reconstructed, resulting in improved freight service in the region.

Construction included:

*   Six rail bridges, constructed to meet state-of-good-repair guidelines
*   18 grade crossings and 14 interlockings
*   Four new stations and a layover facility for storing trains overnight
*   Signal systems and [positive train control (PTC)](https://www.mbta.com/projects/commuter-rail-positive-train-control-ptc) for the entire Phase 1 corridor

Work took place in Middleborough, Taunton, Lakeville, Freetown, and New Bedford. Testing for the entire South Coast Rail occurred under this contract.

Work has been completed on the Fall River Secondary Line to overlay signals and communications.

[See a map of the Middleborough Secondary and New Bedford lines](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/2020-05/SCR_MSNBML_map.pdf)

[Read the press release](https://www.mbta.com/news/2020-08-24/fmcb-approves-4035-million-contract-south-coast-rail-main-line-construction)

The Full Build will extend Commuter Rail service on the Stoughton Main Line and Northeast Corridor (north of Canton Junction). It will bring service to Taunton and connect more communities in the region.

This stage presents more challenges related to wetland impacts, complex engineering, electrification, and cost. The next steps include starting conceptual design work, preliminary engineering, and securing funding.

[See a map of the Full Build corridor](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/2020-05/SCR_FullBuild_CorridorMap_2020.pdf) (PDF, 793 KB)

Past Events

| | The **Fall River/New Bedford Line** (formerly the **Middleborough/Lakeville Line**) is a [commuter rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commuter_rail "Commuter rail") line of the [MBTA Commuter Rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail "MBTA Commuter Rail") system in southeastern [Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts "Massachusetts"), United States. It runs south from [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston") to [Taunton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton,_Massachusetts "Taunton, Massachusetts"), where it splits into branches to [Fall River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River,_Massachusetts "Fall River, Massachusetts") and [New Bedford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bedford,_Massachusetts "New Bedford, Massachusetts"). There are 10 intermediate stations on the combined section and one on each branch. With a distance of 60 miles (97 km) from Boston to New Bedford and 56.6 miles (91.1 km) to Fall River, it is the second-longest line in the system. Most of the line originated as the [Fall River Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River_Railroad_/(1846/) "Fall River Railroad (1846)"), which opened in segments between Fall River and [South Braintree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braintree_station_/(MBTA/) "Braintree station (MBTA)") via Middleborough in 1845 and 1846. At South Braintree, it met the [Old Colony Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#Old_Colony_Railroad_\(1844%E2%80%931854\) "Old Colony Railroad"), which provided a connection to Boston. The two railroads merged in 1854 to form the [Old Colony and Fall River Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_and_Fall_River_Railroad "Old Colony and Fall River Railroad"). While the [Dighton and Somerset Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dighton_and_Somerset_Railroad "Dighton and Somerset Railroad") largely replaced the line as a Boston–Fall River route in 1866, it remained busy with commuter and Boston–[Cape Cod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod "Cape Cod") traffic. Mergers brought it under the [Old Colony Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad "Old Colony Railroad") in 1872 and the [New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York,_New_Haven_and_Hartford_Railroad "New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad") in 1893. Commuter service peaked in the early 20th century and began to decline in the 1910s. Service on the Fall River–Middleborough segment ended in 1931. After two decades of attempts to end Old Colony Division service, the New Haven terminated it in 1959. Planning for the [Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Transportation_Authority "Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority") to restore service on the Middleborough line began in the 1970s. Construction began in 1993, and service on the Middleborough/Lakeville Line began in 1997. Seasonal [CapeFlyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CapeFlyer "CapeFlyer") excursion service began using the line in 2013. The line was extended and renamed in 2025 as part of the first phase of the [South Coast Rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail "South Coast Rail") project. An extension from Middleborough to [Buzzards Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buzzards_Bay_station "Buzzards Bay station") or [Bourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourne_station "Bourne station") is proposed. Maximum speeds are 79 miles per hour (127 km/h) south of Braintree and 59 miles per hour (95 km/h) to the north.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-transitmatters-3): 12 [\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-dseir-2): 53  The line is mostly single track with passing sidings; there is some double track in Boston, Quincy, Braintree, and Brockton, and between Cotley Junction and Myricks Junction.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-transitmatters-3): 11 [\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-dseir-2): 52  Layover yards for the line are located in Fall River and New Bedford, plus an older yard in Middleborough.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-dseir-2): 7, 47  All stations are [accessible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accessible "Accessible") with full-length high-level platforms.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-transitmatters-3): 10 [\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-dseir-2): 56–58 As of October 2025, the portion between East Taunton and Boston has 16 round trips on weekdays and 13 on weekends. For the 1961 season, Boston–Cape Cod service ran via Stoughton.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem3-28): 26  The New York trains ran until 1964.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-lynch-30) Freight service continued to use the Middleborough line.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-sne-6): 404 The [Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Transportation_Authority "Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority") (MBTA) was formed in August 1964 as an expansion of the urban Metropolitan Transit Authority into the surrounding suburbs. The MBTA was intended to subsidize commuter rail service – and to replace much of it with rapid transit extensions.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 13  The MBTA's first such project was a branch of the [Red Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Line_/(MBTA/) "Red Line (MBTA)") (Cambridge–Dorchester Line) following the Old Colony alignment to Braintree.[\[e\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-35) In November 1965, the MBTA purchased the Old Colony main line between Boston and South Braintree from the New Haven.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-36)[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-clarke-32): 22  By 1966, the MBTA expected to eventually extend the line to Braintree Highlands or Holbrook on the Middleborough line, with a spur to [Weymouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weymouth,_Massachusetts "Weymouth, Massachusetts") or [Hingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hingham,_Massachusetts "Hingham, Massachusetts").[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-clarke-32): 24  The Red Line opened to [Quincy Center station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincy_Center_station "Quincy Center station") in September 1971 and [Braintree station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braintree_station_/(MBTA/) "Braintree station (MBTA)") in South Braintree in March 1980.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-netransit-5)[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem3-28): 36  Within Boston, a single freight track paralleled the new tracks. Although there was no freight service through Quincy, a single-track right-of-way was reserved for future freight use when the extension was built.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem3-28): 36 [\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-clarke-32): i, 1, 4 The New Haven Railroad merged into [Penn Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penn_Central "Penn Central") at the end of 1968.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 15  In 1970, following [revolts against freeways in the urban core](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highway_revolts_in_the_United_States#Massachusetts "Highway revolts in the United States"), Massachusetts governor [Francis Sargent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Sargent "Francis Sargent") placed a moratorium on new highway construction inside the [Route 128 beltway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Route_128 "Massachusetts Route 128"). The resulting cancellation of the [Southwest Expressway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwest_Corridor_/(Massachusetts/)#Highway_proposal "Southwest Corridor (Massachusetts)") by the [Boston Transportation Planning Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Transportation_Planning_Review "Boston Transportation Planning Review") meant the already-overcrowded Southeast Expressway would continue to be the only highway into Boston from the south.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem3-28): 36 [\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 16  In January 1973, the MBTA acquired most of Penn Central's suburban lines around Boston, including the Middleborough line as far south as Campello.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-37)[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-38)[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-39) [![Image 132: A passenger train crossing a high girder bridge over a river](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/MBTA_Commuter_Rail_train_on_George_L._Anderson_Bridge_November_2025.jpg/250px-MBTA_Commuter_Rail_train_on_George_L._Anderson_Bridge_November_2025.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MBTA_Commuter_Rail_train_on_George_L._Anderson_Bridge_November_2025.jpg) A major part of the Old Colony Lines restoration was the George L. Anderson Bridge over the Neponset River. A 1974 state report evaluated potential service as far as Hyannis and Falmouth on Cape Cod. It estimated construction costs of $13.6 million to $23 million (equivalent to $67–113 million in 2024), plus $9.2 million ($45 million) for purchasing the tracks and $2.5 to $6.8 million ($12–34 million) for equipment.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-40) On October 15, 1979, a special train ran from Braintree to Middleborough to publicize the state's plans for restored service.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-secondsection-41) In 1984, a state-directed MBTA study found that restoration of commuter rail service on the former Old Colony lines would be feasible.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-ES-42): 4  During the summers of 1984 to 1988, the [Cape Cod and Hyannis Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod_and_Hyannis_Railroad "Cape Cod and Hyannis Railroad") operated passenger service between Braintree station and Cape Cod. Intended partially as a precursor to full commuter rail service, it made five intermediate stops (Holbrook, Brockton, Bridgewater, Middleborough, and Wareham) between Braintree and Buzzards Bay.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-43)[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-anew-44)[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-45) A Draft Environmental Impact Statement (DEIS) for restoration of service on the Middleborough, Plymouth, and Greenbush lines was released in May 1990.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-46) In 1991, the state agreed to build a set of transit projects as part of an agreement with the [Conservation Law Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservation_Law_Foundation "Conservation Law Foundation") (CLF), which had threatened a lawsuit over auto emissions from the Central Artery/Tunnel Project ([Big Dig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Dig "Big Dig")). Among these projects was the "Old Colony Commuter Rail Line Extension", to be complete by the end of 1996.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-1991agreement-47)[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-48)[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-49) The Final Environmental Impact Statement for the Middleborough and Plymouth lines – often called the "Old Colony Lines" – was released in 1992.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-50)[\[f\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-51) Two station sites considered in the DEIS – Westdale in West Bridgewater and Middleborough/[Route 44](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Route_44 "Massachusetts Route 44") in northern Middleborough – were dropped from consideration.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-ES-42): 4 Construction of the $560 million project began in 1993, with service then expected to begin in late 1996.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-52) Which stations to include on the shared mainline between Braintree and Boston proved controversial. Original plans called only for a stop at Braintree.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-ES-42): 8  In September 1995, state governor [Bill Weld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Weld "Bill Weld") announced that a platform would be built at [Quincy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincy_Center_station "Quincy Center station") instead.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-53) Later that year, the MBTA agreed to build both stations.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-54) In November 1996, the MBTA agreed to add a stop at [JFK/UMass station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JFK/UMass_station "JFK/UMass station") as well.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-bypass-55) Limited weekday service with four daily round trips each on the Middleborough/Lakeville Line and [Plymouth/Kingston Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plymouth/Kingston_Line "Plymouth/Kingston Line") began on September 29, 1997.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-56)[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-57) Full service began on November 30, 1997. The Middleborough/Lakeville Line had twelve round trips on weekdays and seven on weekends.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-58)[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-59) Weekend and some weekday trains began stopping at JFK/UMass on April 30, 2001.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-netransit-5)[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-bypass-55) [![Image 133: A diesel locomotive leading a passenger train into a suburban station with a curved high-level platform](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7b/Outbound_train_entering_Middleborough-Lakeville_MBTA_station%2C_Lakeville_MA.jpg/250px-Outbound_train_entering_Middleborough-Lakeville_MBTA_station%2C_Lakeville_MA.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Outbound_train_entering_Middleborough-Lakeville_MBTA_station,_Lakeville_MA.jpg) A train at Middleborough/Lakeville in 2013 In 2007, [concrete ties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concrete_sleeper "Concrete sleeper") used on the Old Colony Lines began to fail due to manufacturing errors. The rate of failures increased during the following two winters, affecting service and causing speed restrictions.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-60) In 2010, the MBTA began a project to replace the 150,000 failing ties, which were part of a batch of 600,000 made in the 1990s, with wooden ties.[\[g\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-62) Some replacement work in Bridgewater and Middleborough took place in 2010.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-beacon-ties-61) Midday service on the Middleborough/Lakeville Line was replaced by buses from March 14 to June 6, 2011.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-june1-63)[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-64) Weekend service on the line was replaced from March 26 to December 18, 2011, and March 17 to April 22, 2012.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-65)[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-june1-63) The project was completed in May 2012 at a cost of $91.5 million.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-66)[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-67) On May 24, 2013, the MBTA began operating [CapeFlyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CapeFlyer "CapeFlyer") service between Boston and Hyannis over the Middleborough Main Line and Cape Main Line. Service consisted of one daily round trip on Friday evenings, Saturdays, and Sundays during the summer tourist season.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-capeflyer2013-68)[\[h\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-70) In 2013 and 2014, the Friday evening southbound train operated as an extension of a regular Middleborough/Lakeville Line train, while Saturday and Sunday service operated with a separate trainset. In 2015, Friday CapeFlyer service also began using a separate trainset.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-capeflyer2013-68)[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-71) Substantially reduced schedules were in effect on the Commuter Rail system from March 16 to June 23, 2020, due to the COVID-19 pandemic.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-netransit-5) Schedule changes effective November 2, 2020, added midday service with consistent 60-to-70-minute midday headways on the Middleborough/Lakeville Line, though a pilot of late-night service was discontinued.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-72) Temporary reduced schedules were again put into place from December 14, 2020, to April 5, 2021.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-73)[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-74) By October 2022, Middleborough/Lakeville service was at 77% of pre-COVID ridership.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-oct2022ridership-1) [![Image 134: A curved high-level railway station platform](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8e/Middleborough_station_near_completion_%281%29%2C_August_2023.jpg/250px-Middleborough_station_near_completion_%281%29%2C_August_2023.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Middleborough_station_near_completion_/(1/),_August_2023.jpg) Middleborough station near completion in August 2023 In the 1980s — during the first expansion of commuter rail service in Massachusetts in decades — the restoration of service to New Bedford and Fall River ([South Coast Rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail "South Coast Rail")) was proposed. Three routes were considered, including the Middleborough Main Line and Middleborough Secondary. By 1988, the MBTA was tentatively planning to use a route via [Stoughton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoughton_station "Stoughton station").[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-75) A 1995 feasibility study found that the limited capacity of the single track between Boston and Braintree could only support service to Fall River or New Bedford, but not both.[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-1995report-76) Planning for the Stoughton route continued until it was suspended in 2003.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-srpedd-77) Planning restarted several years later. The 2009 alternatives analysis report, 2011 draft [environmental impact statement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_impact_statement "Environmental impact statement"), and 2013 final environmental impact statement all chose the Stoughton route.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-78)[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-DEIS-79)[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-FEIS-80) In June 2016, the MBTA announced that the project cost had been revised to $3.42 billion, with completion not expected until 2030. The substantial delay and increase in cost caused officials to consider alternate plans, including an interim service to New Bedford via Middleborough. Some local and regional officials objected to that plan, as it would have reduced service to Middleborough/Lakeville station and potentially interfered with Plymouth/Kingston Line and Greenbush Line service.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-june2016-81)[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-82) In March 2017, the state announced a revised plan intended to provide service sooner for a total cost of $3.42 billion. The $1.1 billion Phase 1 would follow the Middleborough route and open in 2024 with service to both Fall River and New Bedford. Phase 2 would follow the Stoughton route (including electrification) and open in 2029.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-gears-83) Middleborough and Lakeville officials were critical of the possibility of abandoning Middleborough/Lakeville station — which had attracted [transit-oriented development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transit-oriented_development "Transit-oriented development") — or requiring its riders to take a shuttle train.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-sharp-84) By June 2017, the Phase 1 completion date was moved to 2022.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-85) The draft supplemental environmental impact report was issued in January 2018. It analyzed three options for Middleborough: a reverse move to serve the existing station, a new Middleborough station with a rail shuttle between the existing station and Bridgewater, and a new Middleborough station with a bus shuttle from the developments at the existing station site. The third option was chosen for higher operational flexibility, lower travel times, and avoiding the need to add double track between Middleborough and Bridgewater.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-dseir-2): 19 The two main construction contracts for the project were awarded in May and August 2020. By then, service was expected to begin in late 2023.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-FRaward-86)[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-87) Overall project completion reached the halfway point in mid-2022.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-88) In September 2023, the MBTA indicated that revenue service would not begin until mid-2024.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-89) In April 2024, the MBTA acknowledged that a midyear opening was unlikely but did not provide a new schedule.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-90)[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-91) In June 2024, the MBTA announced that the planned opening had been delayed again to May 2025.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-92)[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-93) Service began on March 24, 2025. The line was renamed as the Fall River/New Bedford Line at that time.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-march24-94)[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-95) Weekday service on the main portion of the line increased from 14 round trips to 16; weekend service increased from 10 round trips to 13.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-scr-schedule-96)[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-97) The months after the extension saw several service quality issues.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-june5-98) A shortage of rail crews caused some trains to be cancelled during the first several weekends.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-june5-98)[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-99) The MBTA preemptively replaced some trips with buses on the weekends of April 19–20 and 26–27.[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-100)[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-101)[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-102) One third of trains were late during the first two weeks of extended service, versus one-tenth systemwide. On-time performance improved thereafter but remained below the rest of the system through April and May. The MBTA blamed "startup conditions" and difficulty coordinating trains on the mostly-single-track line for the issues.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-june5-98) On July 21, 2025, the schedule was changed to improve reliability. This included removal of off-peak and weekend stops at JFK/UMass, removal of two late-night shuttle trains, and longer running times.[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-103)[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-104) By November 2025, daily ridership on the line was about 2,000 higher than a year before.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-105) ### Cape Cod service proposals \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line&action=edit§ion=11 "Edit section: Cape Cod service proposals")\] [![Image 135: A Spanish revival style railway station](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9d/Buzzards_Bay_station_HDR.jpg/250px-Buzzards_Bay_station_HDR.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Buzzards_Bay_station_HDR.jpg) [Buzzards Bay station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buzzards_Bay_station "Buzzards Bay station"), a possible future terminus of service In 2007, the Boston Region Metropolitan Planning Organization released a feasibility study of extending commuter rail service to [Buzzards Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buzzards_Bay,_Massachusetts "Buzzards Bay, Massachusetts"), a portion of [Bourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourne,_Massachusetts "Bourne, Massachusetts") on the north side of the [Cape Cod Canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod_Canal "Cape Cod Canal"). Intermediate stops were to be at Rock Village in southern Middleborough, County Road on the [Rochester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rochester,_Massachusetts "Rochester, Massachusetts")/[Wareham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wareham,_Massachusetts "Wareham, Massachusetts") border, and [downtown Wareham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wareham_Village_station "Wareham Village station").[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-2007study-106) The introduction of the CapeFLYER brought new attention to the possibility of extending the Middleborough/Lakeville Line to Buzzards Bay.[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-possibility-107) Later in 2013, the Wareham Chamber of Commerce and Buzzards Bay town selectmen both indicated support for Buzzards Bay commuter rail based on the success of the CapeFLYER, the Chamber supported the extension of commuter rail service to [Buzzards Bay station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buzzards_Bay_station "Buzzards Bay station").[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-108)[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-109) [MassDOT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MassDOT "MassDOT") and the Cape Cod Commission both studied the potential service in 2014–15. The studies estimated daily ridership of 800 to 875 if all Middleborough/Lakeville trains were extended to Buzzards Bay without intermediate stops.[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-2015study-110) Bourne voted to join the MBTA district in 2015 and began paying an [assessment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_assessment "Tax assessment") in mid-2016, although there was no guarantee that commuter rail service would be provided.[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-111) MassDOT began planning a possible trial service in October 2015. The service was to have shuttle trains between Bourne and Middleborough/Lakeville operated by [Massachusetts Coastal Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Coastal_Railroad "Massachusetts Coastal Railroad").[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-rausch-112) The MBTA Fiscal Management and Control Board rejected the service proposal in April 2016.[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-113) During the South Coast Rail project, Middleborough station was designed with space for a shuttle platform to be added later.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-dseir-2): 38  In 2021, MassDOT released a feasibility study of Cape Cod commuter rail service. Middleborough–Buzzards Bay shuttle service with seven daily round trips was expected to have 1,710 total daily boardings, while Middleborough–[Bourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourne_station "Bourne station") service with ten daily round trips (including two off-peak Boston round trips) was expected to have 2,540 total daily boardings. Service to Hyannis was not evaluated because the Bourne–Hyannis segment would require significant track and signal improvements to be suitable for commuter service.[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-114) 1. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_ref-8)** Until August 1846, its name was the United Corporation of the Middleborough Railroad Corporation with the Fall River Branch Railroad Company and the Randolph and Bridgewater Railroad Corporation.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-sne-6): 403 [\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-7) 2. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_ref-12)** The Boston–Braintree main line was double-tracked in 1848; the northern portion was quadruple-tracked in the early 20th century.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 95  3. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_ref-17)** Two trains used the West Bridgewater Branch and [Stoughton Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoughton_Branch "Stoughton Branch"); one used the [Bridgewater Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bridgewater_Branch&action=edit&redlink=1 "Bridgewater Branch (page does not exist)") and the Plymouth main line. Six additional trains operated from Bridgewater to Boston using the Bridgewater Branch.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 34, 96  4. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_ref-23)** Those on the Middleborough line were Matfield, Westdale, and Stanley – all between Brockton and Middleboro. [Rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough/Lakeville_station#History "Middleborough/Lakeville station"), [South Middleboro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough/Lakeville_station#History "Middleborough/Lakeville station"), and [Tremont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tremont_station_/(Massachusetts/) "Tremont station (Massachusetts)") were all between Middleborough and Wareham.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-wouldclose-22)[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem1-20): 19  5. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_ref-35)** Part of the Cambridge–Dorchester Line had previously been constructed along a section of the main line plus the [Shawmut Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shawmut_Branch_Railroad "Shawmut Branch Railroad") in the 1920s.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 96  A rapid transit extension to Braintree had been proposed by regional plans in 1926 and 1945.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-1926report-33)[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-34) That plan was overwhelmingly rejected by Quincy and Braintree voters in 1948.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem2-27): 10–12  Not until Old Colony service ended did the plan gain traction.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem3-28): 29 [\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-clarke-32): 1  6. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_ref-51)** Unlike the other two lines, the Greenbush Line involved reactivation of abandoned right-of-way, and it proved more controversial. The MBTA moved forward with the Middleborough and Plymouth lines; after significant controversy, the Greenbush Line ultimately opened in 2007.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-ES-42): 5 [\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem3-28): 37 [\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-netransit-5) 7. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_ref-62)** [Amtrak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amtrak "Amtrak") and the [Long Island Rail Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island_Rail_Road "Long Island Rail Road") also had to replace large numbers of ties from that batch.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-beacon-ties-61) 8. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_ref-70)** For the 2013 season, the service ran until [Columbus Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Day "Columbus Day") weekend in mid-October.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-permanent-69) 1. ^ [_**a**_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_ref-oct2022ridership_1-0) [_**b**_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_ref-oct2022ridership_1-1) Poftak, Steve (October 27, 2022). 4.content:
Project Overview
----------------

South Coast Rail will be built in phases. Phase 1 service will provide a one-seat ride by extending the existing Middleborough/Lakeville commuter rail service from Boston to Taunton, Fall River and New Bedford.

Elements of Phase 1:

*   Uses the Middleborough Secondary (currently a freight line) to provide service to Taunton, New Bedford, and Fall River. The Middleborough Secondary connects to Cotley Junction in East Taunton.
*   From Cotley Junction, Phase 1 trains will join the New Bedford Main Line and continue to New Bedford, or they will branch off on the Fall River Secondary to Fall River (this area is known as the Southern Triangle).

Benefits of Phase 1:

*   Reconstructs 12.1 miles of the Fall River Secondary
*   Reconstructs 24.1 miles of Middleborough Secondary and the New Bedford Main Line.
*   Improves freight service to the region and will provide redundancy for commuter rail riders once the Full Build is operating.

The Full Build Project will travel on the Stoughton Main Line and Northeast Corridor (north of Canton Junction). The Full Build presents more challenges related to wetland impacts, complex engineering, electrification and cost.

Phase 1 and Full Build
----------------------

To provide service to southeastern Massachusetts, South Coast Rail will be constructed in phases.

### Phase 1 Project

*   Extends Commuter Rail service on the Middleborough/Lakeville Line to New Bedford, Fall River, and Taunton.
*   Phase 1 is fully funded with $1B in State revenue bonds, and construction is complete.

### Full Build Project

*   Extends Commuter Rail service on the Stoughton Line to the New Bedford and Fall River lines, connecting more communities, including Easton and Raynham, to Boston.
*   Funding has not yet been identified for the Full Build program.

For more details, see the Phase 1 and Full Build [corridor maps](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/south-coast-rail-project-corridor-maps).

Phase 1 station locations
-------------------------

Phase 1 will continue service to nine existing stations on the Middleborough/Lakeville line and will add six new stations including:

*   Middleborough
*   East Taunton
*   Freetown
*   Fall River Depot
*   Church Street in New Bedford
*   New Bedford

For the exact locations of each station see the Phase 1 and Full Build [corridor maps](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/south-coast-rail-project-corridor-maps).

All stations will comply with MBTA standards and the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) requirements, which include high-level platforms for "all-doors" boarding. Other amenities will include benches, canopies, bicycle storage and parking.

Phase 1 projected service
-------------------------

(subject to change)
| Line | Original Project Commitment | MBTA Delivery |
| --- | --- | --- |
| East Taunton-South Station | **26** | **32** |
| Fall River Line | **13** | **15** |
| New Bedford Line | **13** | **17** |
| Weekends | **\-** | **26** |

\*Direct trips to/from South Station\*

*   In addition to direct service, there will also be shuttles operating between each terminus point and East Taunton Station; this allows for even more frequent service, which is consistent with the All Day Service model across the rest of the Commuter Rail network
*   Weekday Direct service will run approximately every 70 minutes
*   Weekend Direct service will run approximately every 120 minutes
*   Late Night Service will be offered to South Coast Rail stations with the last train leaving Boston just before mid-night

Noise program eligibility
-------------------------

MassDOT evaluated noise levels anticipated from South Coast Rail trains according to Federal Transit Administration (FTA) guidelines and detailed the results in the [2013 Final Environmental Impact Statement/Report](https://www.mass.gov/lists/south-coast-rail-documents-and-meeting-materials#full-build-final-environmental-impact-statement/report-\(feis/r\)---august-2013-) and the [2018 Final Supplemental Environmental Impact Report](https://www.mass.gov/lists/south-coast-rail-documents-and-meeting-materials#phase-1-final-supplemental-environmental-impact-report-\(fseir\)---april-2018-). While freight trains currently operate along the existing railroad corridor, they are infrequent. The Commuter Rail trains will run multiple trips every day, which creates additional noise. The MBTA developed and implemented a noise mitigation program based on the FTA standards.

Based on this program, the MBTA has provided funding for a set of alternative noise mitigation measures to owners of properties that are affected by noise above the impact level. See the [South Coast Rail Noise Program Frequently Asked Questions](https://www.mass.gov/doc/scr-noise-mitigation-program-faq/download) for more information.

Construction impacts, timeline and contracts
--------------------------------------------

### Early Action Construction

MassDOT began Early Action construction projects in 2019 on South Coast Rail to prepare for the larger Phase 1 main line rail construction contracts. The first visible active construction projects were drainage culvert replacement and a major railroad grade crossing update in New Bedford. This work also included the construction of 5 wetland mitigation areas in the corridor and was substantially completed in Summer 2020. Additional work to replace four railroad bridges was completed in Fall 2020. The Early Action took place in Berkley, Fall River, Freetown, Lakeville, Middleborough, New Bedford, Raynham, and Taunton.

More information can be found on the [SCR Construction Activity](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/south-coast-rail-construction-activity) page.

### Early Demolition Contract

The Early Demolition contract was awarded to DW White Construction of Acushnet and was completed in Fall 2020. This work involved the demolition of buildings and other structures located on MBTA controlled property at nine separate locations in Middleborough, Taunton, Berkley, Freetown, Fall River, and New Bedford.

### Fall River Secondary Line Construction

This construction contract was [awarded to Skanska DW White JV](https://www.mbta.com/news/2020-05-11/fmcb-approves-159-million-contract-south-coast-rail-main-line-construction) on May 11, 2020. Work on the Fall River Secondary will include track, stations, bridges, and a layover facility. Construction began Summer 2020 and is complete.

### New Bedford, Middleborough, Signal and Communications Contract

This construction contract was [awarded to SCR Constructors JV](https://www.mbta.com/news/2020-08-24/fmcb-approves-4035-million-contract-south-coast-rail-main-line-construction) on August 24, 2020. Work on the New Bedford Main Line to the Middleborough Secondary includes track, stations, bridges, a layover facility, and the signal and communications systems for all of Phase 1. Construction began in fall 2020 and is complete.

Public outreach
---------------

The South Coast Rail team has conducted numerous public meetings across the Phase 1 project communities. The project team will continue to meet with the cities and towns as needed.

In addition to specific railroad safety measures, education is a key factor in addressing community safety. The South Coast Rail Project funded the development of instructive videos for railroad safety, geared to schools and the general public. This effort is supplemented by Operation Lifesaver volunteers. MassDOT and the MBTA work regularly with [Operation Lifesaver](https://oli.org/), a national program sponsored by the Federal Railroad Administration (FRA), that provides community railroad safety education programs.

The MBTA and Keolis, the MBTA’s Commuter Rail operator, has been working with South Coast Rail community first responders to conduct regular emergency response drills and training.

**Service begins on the new Fall River/New Bedford Commuter Rail Line on March 24.**

* * *

BOSTON – The MBTA today announced that South Coast Rail schedules are now available for the Fall River/New Bedford Commuter Rail Line. For the first time in 65 years, the communities of Taunton, Freetown, New Bedford, Middleborough, and Fall River will now have passenger rail service to and from downtown Boston. [Service begins Monday, March 24](https://www.mbta.com/news/2025-02-07/mbta-announces-south-coast-rail-service-begins-march-24-2025), with schedules available on [mbta.com](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/media/route_pdfs/batch_7394/2025-03-24-cr-spring-summer-fall-river-new-bedford-line.pdf).

“The launch of South Coast Rail passenger service underscores the Healey-Driscoll Administration’s commitment to delivering safe, reliable, accessible, and resilient transportation infrastructure for the residents and businesses of Massachusetts,” **said Transportation Secretary and CEO Monica Tibbits-Nutt**. “We deeply appreciate the public’s patience, the collaboration of local officials, and the dedication of our employees and contractors, all of whom made this milestone possible. With service beginning on March 24, thousands of cars will come off the roads, and thousands of people will experience the convenience and benefits of public transportation firsthand.”

"We’re pleased to welcome our new south coast passengers to the Commuter Rail with the release of the new schedules that go into effect on March 24,” **said MBTA General Manager and CEO Phillip Eng**. "This is another important milestone as we bring rail service to southeastern Massachusetts communities after 65 years, offering new and exciting opportunities for residents and visitors in this region. We sincerely appreciate the patience and support from stakeholders and community members, the collaboration from our state and federal partners, and I couldn’t be more grateful to the many teams at the MBTA and our industry partners who are making this a reality.”

South Coast Rail Schedules  
----------------------------

Fifteen trips will operate on the Fall River Commuter Rail Line and 17 trips will operate on the New Bedford Commuter Rail Line with a total of 32 trips between South Station and East Taunton. There will be a total of 26 trips between South Station and East Taunton on the weekends. Trains will run every 70 minutes on weekdays and every 2 hours on the weekends.

Late-night service will be offered to South Coast Rail stations with the last train leaving Boston just before midnight.

In addition to direct service, there will also be connecting trains operating between each terminus point and East Taunton Station. This allows for even more frequent service, which is consistent with the all-day service model across the rest of the Commuter Rail network.

Full schedules are available now at [mbta.com](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/media/route_pdfs/batch_7394/2025-03-24-cr-spring-summer-fall-river-new-bedford-line.pdf).

Commuter Rail Line and Station Renaming, Other Changes  
--------------------------------------------------------

Passengers are reminded that the Middleborough/Lakeville Commuter Rail Line will be renamed the Fall River/New Bedford Commuter Rail Line when service begins on March 24.

Middleborough/Lakeville station (located at 125 Commercial Drive, Lakeville) will be renamed Lakeville Station.

Commuter Rail trains will no longer stop at Lakeville Station. The Lakeville Station will serve only the seasonal [CapeFLYER](https://capeflyer.com/).

The new Middleborough Station (located at 52 West Grove Street, Middleborough) will serve the Commuter Rail.

Fares  
-------

All South Coast Rail stations are [Zone 8 stations](https://www.mbta.com/fares/commuter-rail-fares). This means that passengers will pay a full fare of $12.25 and a reduced fare of $6 for a one-way ride between Zone 1A to 8.

Free Weekend Service and Parking This Spring 
---------------------------------------------

As previously announced, free weekend service and parking will be available from March 29 and April 27.

*   Free Weekend Service  Fare-free service will be available on the Fall River/New Bedford Commuter Rail Lines for all weekends (Saturdays and Sundays) between March 29 and April 27 as well as on April 21 (Patriots’ Day). Passengers can ride for free if they are boarding or ending their ride at one of the six South Coast Rail stations.
    
    Riders should share their origin and destination stations with conductors to receive free travel. This offer is only valid on the Fall River and New Bedford Commuter Rail Lines and does not apply to trains on other Commuter Rail lines.
    
    On weekdays, regular Commuter Rail fares are in effect for South Coast Rail.
    
*   Free Parking Commuter Rail parking at the six South Coast Rail station lots – Middleborough, East Taunton, Freetown, Church Street, Fall River Depot, and New Bedford – will be free March 24 through the end of the day on April 30, 2025.
    
    This free parking promotion may end earlier than anticipated if South Coast Rail parking lots fill up and spaces become unavailable. Standard parking rates for South Coast Rail stations are $4 per day on weekdays and $2 per day on weekends/holidays.
    

Media Contact Information
-------------------------

For questions or comments about this press release, please contact:

MBTA Press Office

Members of the press can request to join our media list by emailing [MediaRelations@mbta.com](mailto:MediaRelations@mbta.com). We'll send you MBTA press releases and media advisories directly.

A Rider’s Guide to the New Fall River/New Bedford Regional Rail Line
====================================================================

[![Image 3](https://lede-admin.mass.streetsblog.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/49/2023/05/PROMO-milneil.png?resize=100%2C100)](https://mass.streetsblog.org/author/christianmilneil)

By [Christian MilNeil](https://mass.streetsblog.org/author/christianmilneil)

11:26 AM EDT on March 24, 2025

*   [Share on Reddit](http://www.reddit.com/submit/?title=A%20Rider%E2%80%99s%20Guide%20to%20the%20New%20Fall%20River%2FNew%20Bedford%20Regional%20Rail%20Line&url=https%3A%2F%2Fmass.streetsblog.org%2F2025%2F03%2F24%2Fa-riders-guide-to-the-new-fall-river-new-bedford-regional-rail-line)
