*   [Share on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle/?summary=On%20Monday%20morning%2C%20the%20MBTA%20debuted%20its%20newest%20rail%20line%3A%20a%20two-branch%20extension%20of%20the%20former%20Middleborough%2FLakeville%20Line%20to%20the%20Bristol%20County%20cities%20of%20New%20Bedford%20and%20Fall%20River.%20Here%26%238217%3Bs%20what%20to%20know%20about%20the%20Commonwealth%26%238217%3Bs%20newest%20transit%20line%3A%20Trains%20every%2070%20minutes%20The%20schedule%20features%20near-hourly%20service%20between%20New%20Bedford%2C%20Fall%20River%2C%20and%20downtown%E2%80%A6%0A&title=A%20Rider%E2%80%99s%20Guide%20to%20the%20New%20Fall%20River%2FNew%20Bedford%20Regional%20Rail%20Line&url=https%3A%2F%2Fmass.streetsblog.org%2F2025%2F03%2F24%2Fa-riders-guide-to-the-new-fall-river-new-bedford-regional-rail-line)
*   [Share on Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fmass.streetsblog.org%2F2025%2F03%2F24%2Fa-riders-guide-to-the-new-fall-river-new-bedford-regional-rail-line)
*   [Share on Email](mailto:?body=https%3A%2F%2Fmass.streetsblog.org%2F2025%2F03%2F24%2Fa-riders-guide-to-the-new-fall-river-new-bedford-regional-rail-line&subject=A%20Rider%E2%80%99s%20Guide%20to%20the%20New%20Fall%20River%2FNew%20Bedford%20Regional%20Rail%20Line)

![Image 4](https://lede-admin.mass.streetsblog.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/49/2025/03/2025-03-04-fall-river-new-bedford-line-map_40c730-e1742830280833.png?w=2880)

On Monday morning, the MBTA debuted its newest rail line: a two-branch extension of the former Middleborough/Lakeville Line to the Bristol County cities of New Bedford and Fall River.

Here's what to know about the Commonwealth's newest transit line:

Trains every 70 minutes
-----------------------

The schedule features near-hourly service between New Bedford, Fall River, and downtown Boston, with the earliest weekday inbound trains departing Fall River and New Bedford at 4:27 and 5:05 a.m., respectively, and the latest trains for both cities departing South Station at 11:59 p.m.

Most trains will run about 70 minutes apart, although some rush-hour trains will run more frequently.

[**View the official timetable here**](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/media/route_pdfs/batch_7394/2025-03-24-cr-spring-summer-fall-river-new-bedford-line.pdf).

The scheduled trip time from both New Bedford and Fall River is approximately 95 minutes, which is faster than most rush-hour driving times between the two cities, but a bit slower than driving with no traffic.

![Image 5: A stylized rail map of the MBTA Fall River/New Bedford Line, with South Station at the top, Braintree in the center, and Fall River in the lower left corner, and New Bedford in the lower edge.](https://lede-admin.mass.streetsblog.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/49/2025/03/2025-03-04-fall-river-new-bedford-line-map.png?w=710)

A diagram of the new Fall River/New Bedford regional rail line. Courtesy of the MBTA.

Shuttle trains between East Taunton and branches
------------------------------------------------

The T is also running connecting shuttle trains between East Taunton and Fall River or New Bedford, with cross-platform transfers at the East Taunton station, to allow for easier connections between Boston and the ends of the new line's two branches.

For instance, if you're riding from New Bedford to Boston, there are direct trains scheduled at 5:55 and 7:25 a.m.

But there will also be a connecting shuttle train that will depart from New Bedford at 6:22 a.m. to take you as far as East Taunton.

From East Taunton, your shuttle will meet up with the 6:35 a.m. train from Fall River, so you can switch trains and continue on to South Station.

[Those shuttles are denoted on the train schedules with purple arrows that indicate a transfer to the waiting train.](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/media/route_pdfs/batch_7394/2025-03-24-cr-spring-summer-fall-river-new-bedford-line.pdf)

Fully accessible stations, bikes allowed on all trains
------------------------------------------------------

The MBTA built 6 new stations for the new rail line, at Middleborough, East Taunton, Freetown, Fall River, Church Street (a park-and-ride station on the north side of New Bedford), and downtown New Bedford.

Thanks to fully accessible, level-boarding platforms at all the new stations, passengers will be allowed to carry bicycles on board all trains that serve the new line.

Note that the former Middleborough/Lakeville station, located on Commercial Drive, will no longer serve commuter rail trains. It will still be a stop on CapeFlyer service during the summer.

Free fares this week, and free weekend rides in April
-----------------------------------------------------

The MBTA's new New Bedford/Fall River regional rail line will offer fare-free service from opening day until the end of March, and will continue to offer fare-free rides every weekend in April.

For other times, the T has also started selling tickets for the Fall River/New Bedford Commuter Rail Line on its [mTicket mobile ticketing app](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/mbta-mticket/id560487958).

The new stations will all be in Zone 8, which means that a full-priced one-way ticket between South Station and Fall River or New Bedford will cost $12.25.

19.content:
On March 24, 2025, the Middleborough/Lakeville Line extended to Taunton, Freetown, New Bedford, and Fall River, expanding Commuter Rail service between southeastern Massachusetts and Boston! The line has been renamed to the [Fall River/New Bedford Line](https://massbytrain.com/lines/fall-river-new-bedford/).

The [Fall River/New Bedford Line](https://massbytrain.com/lines/fall-river-new-bedford/) offers six newly constructed and accessible stations, connecting communities between Boston and the South Coast of Massachusetts. Skip the traffic, save time and money, and try taking the Fall River/New Bedford Line!

Free Fares at New Stations Every Weekend through May
----------------------------------------------------

**To celebrate the new Fall River/New Bedford Line, the Commuter Rail will offer free weekend service.**

For every weekend (Saturdays and Sundays) between April 5 to May 31, on April 21 (Patriots’ Day) and May 26 (Memorial Day), the Fall River/New Bedford Line will offer fare-free service. Passengers can ride for free if they board or end their ride at one of the six new stations on the Fall River/New Bedford Line. This offer is valid for on-board purchases. Please speak with the conductor about your origin and destination stations. This offer only applies for those on the Fall River and New Bedford Commuter Rail Lines and does not apply to trains on other Commuter Rail Lines. Weekdays operate as regular Commuter Rail fares.

Parking is also free at six of the Fall River/New Bedford Line station lots from March 24 until the end of day on April 30, 2025:

*   [Middleborough](https://massbytrain.com/stations/middleborough/)
*   [East Taunton](https://massbytrain.com/stations/east-taunton/)
*   [Freetown](https://massbytrain.com/stations/freetown/)
*   [Church Street](https://massbytrain.com/stations/church-street/)
*   [Fall River Depot](https://massbytrain.com/stations/fall-river-depot/)
*   [New Bedford](https://massbytrain.com/stations/new-bedford/)

_\*Note: This free parking promotion might end earlier if Fall River/New Bedford Line parking lots fill up and spaces become unavailable. The standard parking rates for these stations are $4 per day on weekdays and $2 per day on weekends/holidays._

![Image 1: Map of the Fall River/New Bedford Line on the Commuter Rail](https://massbytrain.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/2025-03-04-fall-river-new-bedford-line-map-181x300.png)

Fall River/New Bedford Line Service Schedules
---------------------------------------------

There are 15 weekday trips on the Fall River Line and 17 trips on the New Bedford Line. On weekends, the [Fall River/New Bedford Line](https://www.mbta.com/schedules/CR-NewBedford/timetable) operates 26 trips between [South Station](https://massbytrain.com/stations/south-station/) and East Taunton. Trains run every 70 minutes on weekdays and every 2 hours on the weekends. The Fall River/New Bedford Line also offers late-night service, with the last train departing Boston around midnight.

In addition to direct service, [East Taunton Station](https://www.mbta.com/stops/place-NBM-0374) serves as a transfer station; additional trains operate between East Taunton and the Fall River and New Bedford branches, offering connections between Boston and both the Fall River and New Bedford branches on most trips.

Changes with the Fall River/New Bedford Commuter Rail Line
----------------------------------------------------------

For regular Commuter Rail passengers, there are a number of changes to take note of:

*   The Middleborough/Lakeville Line is now called the Fall River/New Bedford Line.
*   The Middleborough/Lakeville Station is now called [Middleborough Station](https://massbytrain.com/stations/middleborough/) and is located at 52 West Grove Street, Middleborough, MA 02346. The former Middleborough/Lakeville station located at 125 Commercial Drive, Lakeville is now Lakeville Station and only serves [CapeFLYER](https://massbytrain.com/special-service/capeflyer/) service.

Fares
-----

All new stations between Middleborough and Fall River or New Bedford operate as Zone 8 Stations. Riders will pay the full fare of $12.25. Riders taking a one-way ride between Zone 1A to 8 will pay a reduced fare of $6.

$10 Holiday Weekend Pass for Memorial Day Weekend
-------------------------------------------------

Get additional unlimited rides on all Commuter Rail Lines during Memorial Day Weekend, May 24-26, 2025. The $10 Weekend Pass covers all zones and stations Saturday, Sunday and Monday during the holiday weekend.

### Former station

#### Early stations

[![Image 1: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Fall_River_station_on_1877_bird%27s_eye_map.jpg/320px-Fall_River_station_on_1877_bird%27s_eye_map.jpg)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#/media/File:Fall_River_station_on_1877_bird's_eye_map.jpg)

Bowenville station (center) on an 1877 map

The [Fall River Railroad](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_Railroad_/(1846/) "Fall River Railroad (1846)") opened from [Myricks](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Myricks,_Massachusetts "Myricks, Massachusetts") to [Fall River](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battleship_Cove_station#History "Battleship Cove station") on June 9, 1845, and to the [Old Colony Railroad](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Old_Colony_Railroad "Old Colony Railroad") at [South Braintree](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Braintree_station_/(MBTA/)#History "Braintree station (MBTA)") in December 1846.[\[4\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-phillips-4)[\[5\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-sne-5): 403  The first Fall River station was located at the south end of a short tunnel under Central Street.[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-6)[\[4\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-phillips-4) It was a two-story building measuring 75 by 180 feet (23 m × 55 m).[\[7\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-shoreliner-7): 19  A temporary depot further north was used until the Central Street tunnel was completed in September 1845.[\[7\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-shoreliner-7): 19  In October 1847, the Fall River and Old Colony began running the Boston–Fall River _Boat Train_, which met [Fall River Line](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_Line "Fall River Line") steamers from New York at the [Fall River Wharf](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battleship_Cove_station#History "Battleship Cove station"); the Central Street station closed at that time.[\[4\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-phillips-4)[\[5\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-sne-5): 403 [\[7\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-shoreliner-7): 19  The two railroads merged as the Old Colony and Fall River Railroad in 1854.[\[5\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-sne-5): 403  The former station was converted to store coal in 1858.[\[7\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-shoreliner-7): 19

In 1862, the railroad began construction of a line south to [Newport, Rhode Island](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Newport,_Rhode_Island "Newport, Rhode Island"). The former station was demolished to make room for the extension.[\[7\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-shoreliner-7): 19  The line to Newport opened in November 1863; the railroad was renamed as the [Old Colony and Newport Railway](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Old_Colony_and_Newport_Railway "Old Colony and Newport Railway").[\[7\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-shoreliner-7): 13  The extension prompted local debate about where to place a station. The railroad preferred a location at [Ferry Street](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battleship_Cove_station#History "Battleship Cove station") south of the wharf, while the city preferred a site near [Metacomet Mill](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Metacomet_Mill "Metacomet Mill") closer to the downtown area.[\[8\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-8)[\[7\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-shoreliner-7): 19  An agreement was eventually made for two stations: one at Ferry Street in the South End, and one near Turner Street in the North End.[\[7\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-shoreliner-7): 19  The Ferry Street station opened by mid-1864; a two-story brick building was built at Maple Street for the North End station, but it never opened as a station.[\[7\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-shoreliner-7): 19 [\[9\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-9)[\[10\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-10)

The [Dighton and Somerset Railroad](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Dighton_and_Somerset_Railroad "Dighton and Somerset Railroad") opened in 1866, joining the Fall River mainline at Somerset Junction, north of Fall River.[\[5\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-sne-5): 393  Trains began stopping at **Bowenville** in the north part of Fall River on August 12, 1867. A wooden station building measuring 18 by 64 feet (5.5 m × 19.5 m) was constructed.[\[11\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-11)[\[12\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-12) The station was named for the nearby neighborhood, itself named for the estate of the Bowen family.[\[7\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-shoreliner-7): 21  The railroad changed names again to become the [Old Colony Railroad](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Old_Colony_Railroad "Old Colony Railroad") in 1872. The Old Colony built a new station building at Bowenville in early 1874 and enlarged it in 1878.[\[4\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-phillips-4)[\[13\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-13)[\[14\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-14)[\[15\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-15) It was located on the east side of the tracks between Turner Street and Old Colony Street.[\[16\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-16)[\[17\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-17) A branch of the [Providence, Warren and Bristol Railroad](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Providence,_Warren_and_Bristol_Railroad "Providence, Warren and Bristol Railroad") (known as the [Fall River, Warren and Providence Railroad](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River,_Warren_and_Providence_Railroad "Fall River, Warren and Providence Railroad")) opened over the new [Slade's Ferry Bridge](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Slade's_Ferry_Bridge "Slade's Ferry Bridge") on December 6, 1875, connecting to the Fall River mainline north of Bowenville.[\[18\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-18) The line was doubled-tracked between Somerset Junction and the Central Street tunnel in 1882; the unused station at Maple Street was demolished at that time.[\[7\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-shoreliner-7): 19 [\[19\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-1882report-19)

#### 1891 station

The [Globe Street Railway](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Old_Colony_Street_Railway "Old Colony Street Railway") opened its first [horsecar](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Horsecar "Horsecar") line on North Main Street between Bowenville and downtown Fall River in July 1880.[\[20\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-20)[\[21\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-21) A short spur on Old Colony Avenue to Bowenville station opened that November.[\[22\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-22) Between the horsecar connection and the northward growth of the city, Bowenville soon became Fall River's main railroad station.[\[23\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-newname-23)[\[24\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-april1890-24) The Old Colony began planning a new station at Pearce Street around 1883. However, the company soon reached an impasse with the city, which desired to open Pearce Street across the tracks and create a new grade crossing.[\[25\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-muddle-25)[\[26\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-26)[\[27\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-27) The street had been legally established in 1873 and laid out in 1874, but the railroad built fences to block access across the tracks.[\[25\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-muddle-25)[\[24\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-april1890-24)

In May 1886, the city alderman ordered the railroad to remove the fences and open the crossing.[\[28\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-28) The Old Colony obtained a temporary injunction; it sought a permanent injunction in July 1886.[\[25\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-muddle-25) That month, the state railroad commissioners issued a report on the dispute. They noted that the existing Bowenville station was responsible for two-thirds of the rail traffic in the city and was inadequate for that purpose. Stating that opening the street in close proximity to a station would "create a grade crossing of the most dangerous kind", the commissioners advised against the construction of a new station if the crossing was opened.[\[24\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-april1890-24) By that time, the railroad was also considering acquisition of the [Fall River Iron Works](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/American_Printing_Company_/(Fall_River_Iron_Works/) "American Printing Company (Fall River Iron Works)") property near the wharf in order to build a central passenger station and freight yard.[\[25\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-muddle-25)

The case was heard by [Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr.](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Oliver_Wendell_Holmes_Jr. "Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr.") for the [Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Massachusetts_Supreme_Judicial_Court "Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court"), which ruled in October 1888 that the city had the right to establish the crossing.[\[29\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-29)[\[30\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-30) Although the Old Colony continued to offer a new station in return for the street being abandoned, the grade crossing was opened on December 28, 1888.[\[31\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-31)[\[32\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-32) The next year, the railroad proposed to build a bridge to carry Pearce Street over the tracks.[\[33\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-33) In April 1890, the Old Colony made a new offer to the city: the railroad would build an underpass to carry [President Avenue](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/U.S._Route_6_in_Massachusetts "U.S. Route 6 in Massachusetts") under the tracks, construct a new station, and pay any damages to abutters for closure of Pearce Street.[\[34\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-34) The city accepted the offer that July; the Pearce Street crossing was closed on August 20.[\[35\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-35)[\[36\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-36)

[![Image 2: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/Fall_River_station_1912_postcard.jpg/640px-Fall_River_station_1912_postcard.jpg)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#/media/File:Fall_River_station_1912_postcard.jpg)

Postcard of the 1891-built station

Plans for the new station by [Bradford Gilbert](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Bradford_Gilbert "Bradford Gilbert") were shown to the public in September 1890. At that time, the railroad yielded to the city's request to use granite rather than brick.[\[37\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-37)[\[38\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-38) Bowenville station was used by 2,000 to 3,000 daily riders by then.[\[39\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-dec11-39) Construction began in December 1890.[\[40\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-40) In August 1891, the railroad announced that the new station would be named **Fall River** since it would be the city's primary passenger station.[\[23\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-newname-23)[\[4\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-phillips-4): 177  Fall River station opened on November 9, 1891. The older Bowenville station building was moved away from the tracks and sold for reuse.[\[41\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-nov9-41) Including land acquisition, the cost of the new station was nearly $100,000 (equivalent to $3.1 million in 2024).[\[42\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-42)

Fall River station was located on the east side of the tracks between Baylies Street and Pearce Street, slightly north of the previous station.[\[43\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-1893sanborn-43) It measured 185 by 40 feet (56 m × 12 m) with rounded ends.[\[39\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-dec11-39) The station was built of [Milford pink granite](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Milford_pink_granite "Milford pink granite") trimmed with [brown sandstone](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Portland_Formation "Portland Formation") from [Longmeadow](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Longmeadow,_Massachusetts "Longmeadow, Massachusetts").[\[44\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-44)[\[39\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-dec11-39) All exposed wood on the exterior was [yellow pine](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Yellow_pine "Yellow pine"). The roof was purple [slate](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Slate "Slate") with dark red [terracotta](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Architectural_terracotta "Architectural terracotta") trim. At its center was a 25-foot (7.6 m)\-square turret with a pyramidal roof.[\[39\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-dec11-39) The station had a single concrete [side platform](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Side_platform "Side platform") used by all passenger trains.[\[41\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-nov9-41)[\[43\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-1893sanborn-43)[\[39\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-dec11-39) It was covered by a canopy attached to the station's roof.[\[39\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-dec11-39)[\[43\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-1893sanborn-43) The Globe Street Railway built a spur track off its North Main Street line to the south end of the station.[\[45\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-45)[\[39\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-dec11-39)

A [porte-cochère](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Porte-coch%C3%A8re "Porte-cochère") projected from the main entrance at the center of the east side of the building. It opened onto a loggia and ticket counter under the 30-foot (9.1 m) ceiling of the turret. Behind the ticket office were the telegraph office and agent's room, each with a [bay window](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Bay_window "Bay window") overlooking the tracks. To each side were the men's and women's waiting rooms, each 37 by 40 feet (11 m × 12 m), with floors and [wainscotting](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Wainscotting "Wainscotting") of dark [red oak](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Red_oak "Red oak"). The women's (north) waiting room had an [inglenook](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Inglenook "Inglenook") around a fireplace on the north wall, flanked by two alcoves that could be screened off for private use. One connected to a [retiring room](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/dictionary/retiring_room "wikt:retiring room") and bathroom. The men's waiting room had an open fireplace on the south wall, with a [smoking room](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Smoking_room "Smoking room") and bathroom connected to the waiting room. Both bathrooms had marble floors and walls. The north end of the station was occupied by the baggage room with the small mail room inside, while the south end held locker rooms for trainmen and [hackmen](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Hackney_carriage "Hackney carriage").[\[39\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-dec11-39)[\[46\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-46)[\[47\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-47)

#### 20th century

The station was raised 8 feet (2.4 m) as part of a 1902–1905 project that eliminated eleven grade crossings in the city.[\[48\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-1911history-48) The New Haven operated [electrified](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Railway_electrification "Railway electrification") passenger service between [Providence](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Providence,_Rhode_Island "Providence, Rhode Island") and Fall River from 1900 to 1934.[\[4\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-phillips-4)[\[49\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-49) Service to Providence, and to Taunton over the Dighton and Somerset, both ended in 1932.[\[5\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-sne-5): 172, 395  Newport service ended in 1938 due to the [88 stations case](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/88_stations_case "88 stations case"); [Ferry Street station](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battleship_Cove_station#History "Battleship Cove station") was closed until around 1950, leaving Fall River as a terminal.[\[5\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-sne-5): 416  Fall River service was suspended from 1949 to 1952, and ultimately ended on September 5, 1958.[\[50\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-150years-50)

### South Coast Rail

[![Image 3: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/14/Wall_construction_at_Fall_River_station%2C_December_2021.jpg/640px-Wall_construction_at_Fall_River_station%2C_December_2021.jpg)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#/media/File:Wall_construction_at_Fall_River_station,_December_2021.jpg)

Retaining wall construction, November 2021

In September 2008, [MassDOT](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/MassDOT "MassDOT") released 18 potential station sites for the [South Coast Rail](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/South_Coast_Rail "South Coast Rail") project, including **Fall River Depot** off Davol Street.[\[51\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-51) A 2009 conceptual design called for a single 730 ft (220 m) [side platform](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Side_platform "Side platform") serving the west track, with a second track allowing freight trains to pass the high-level platform; a two-story parking deck would be located on the west side of the tracks.[\[52\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-52) Plans released as part of the Final Environmental Impact Report in 2013 were nearly identical.[\[53\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-53) A 2009 corridor plan called for [mixed-use](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Mixed-use_development "Mixed-use development") [transit-oriented development](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Transit-oriented_development "Transit-oriented development") around the new station.[\[54\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-54) On June 11, 2010, the state took ownership of the Fall River Subdivision and several other [CSX](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/CSX_Transportation "CSX Transportation") lines as part of a sale agreement.[\[55\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-55)

In 2017, the project was re-evaluated due to cost issues. A new proposal released in March 2017 called for early service via Middleborough by 2024, followed by full service via Stoughton by 2029.[\[56\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-gears-56) The January 2018 _Draft Supplemental Environmental Impact Report_ reconfigured the planned parking lot configuration, as part of the previously planned deck site had been developed for use by a business. A parking lot on the west side of the tracks was to be constructed during Phase 1, with a possible eastern lot (on the site of an existing retail building) to be added later.[\[1\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-dseir-1): 44

The MBTA awarded a $159 million contract for construction of the Fall River Secondary portion of the project, including Fall River station, in May 2020. Service was then planned to begin in November 2023.[\[57\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-FRaward-57)[\[58\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-58) Two former industrial buildings were demolished in 2020 to make room for the station and its parking lot.[\[59\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-59)[\[60\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-60) The station was 32% complete by February 2022, with 96% of platform foundations and some retaining walls in place.[\[61\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-61) Construction of the station reached 90% completion in October 2022, with the platform and canopies in place.[\[62\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-62)[\[63\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-fall2022factsheet-63)[\[64\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-64) Substantial completion of the Fall River Secondary work was announced in December 2022.[\[65\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-65) Opening was delayed to mid-2024 in September 2023.[\[66\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-66) In June 2024, the opening of the project was delayed to May 2025. Fall River station was complete by that time.[\[2\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-may2025-2) Service began on March 24, 2025.[\[67\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fall_River_station#cite_note-march24-67)

2.content:
The Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA) shared today the South Coast Rail passenger service start date.

Pending final approval from the Federal Railroad Administration (FRA), passenger service will begin Monday, March 24, 2025. For the first time in 65 years, the communities of Taunton, Freetown, New Bedford, Middleboro, and Fall River will have passenger rail service

The MBTA will host a public meeting in Freetown on Monday, February 10 at 6 pm with the community. This public gathering follows three previous community meetings hosted in Taunton, Fall River and New Bedford.

“The people of Taunton, Freetown, New Bedford, Middleboro and Fall River have been waiting for passenger rail service for far too long,” **said Governor Maura Healey**. “General Manager Eng and his team aren’t kicking the can down the road – they're delivering. We’re thrilled to soon be launching South Coast Rail service, which will make it easier for South Coast residents to get around the state, reduce congestion and spur economic development.”

“We’re grateful for all of the input and partnership we’ve received from South Coast residents and businesses that have made this milestone possible,” **said Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll**. “This project will bring better commutes while also supporting new jobs, housing and economic growth. We’re grateful for the hard work of MBTA and MassDOT teams to get this done.”

“The Healey-Driscoll administration has fully committed to expanding public transportation in Massachusetts, which includes engaging with our communities, launching studies, applying for grants, investing in infrastructure, and successfully bringing projects like South Coast Rail to fruition,” **said Transportation Secretary and CEO Monica Tibbits-Nutt**. “To everyone who thought the day would never arrive when passenger trains would run again between Fall River, New Bedford, and Boston, we are excited to announce that the day has finally come. South Coast Rail will create opportunities for affordable housing access, connect people to jobs, stimulate regional economies, and encourage a shift from cars to public transportation.”

“Under the leadership of the Healey-Driscoll Administration, we continue to improve mass transportation across our network to make it the preferred choice of travel. Delivering new rail service to the communities as part of South Coast Rail is another example of our workforce fulfilling commitments made to the public. The MBTA is proud to be in this position working collaboratively with the Federal Railroad Administration as we now seek their approval to begin passenger train service at the end of March ahead of our May target. This will allow communities in Boston, southeastern Massachusetts, and many in between to connect by train for the first time in decades,” **said MBTA General Manager and CEO Phillip Eng**. “We sincerely appreciate the patience and support from stakeholders and community members as we performed train testing and conductor training. The residents of the Commonwealth and all of its visitors deserve this service, and I couldn’t be more grateful to the many teams at the MBTA and our industry partners who are making this a reality.”

“Six stations are complete, over 800 safety functions have been tested on the trains, and now operators are beginning to get ready to learn the routes. It hasn’t been an easy feat, but I’m proud of how much we have accomplished,” **said MBTA South Coast Rail Program Executive Karen Antion**. “The South Coast Rail is going to be a gamechanger for the region, and we’re excited to deliver this new transportation option that will serve so many communities.”

**Train schedule**

There will be a total of 15 trips on the Fall River line and 17 trips on the New Bedford Line with a total of 32 trips between South Station and East Taunton. There will be a total of 26 trips between South Station and East Taunton on the weekends. The MBTA anticipates trains to run every 70 minutes on weekdays and every 2 hours on the weekends.

Late night service will be offered to South Coast Rail stations with the last train leaving Boston just before midnight.

In addition to direct service, there will also be shuttles operating between each terminus point and East Taunton Station. This allows for even more frequent service, which is consistent with the All Day Service model across the rest of the Commuter Rail network.

**Train station renaming**

*   When service begins, the Middleborough/Lakeville Line will be renamed the Fall River/New Bedford Line.  
*   The Middleborough/Lakeville Station (located at 125 Commercial Drive, Lakeville) will be renamed Lakeville Station.  
*   Commuter Rail trains will no longer stop at Lakeville Station 
*   The Lakeville Station will serve only the seasonal Cape Cod Flyer.  
*   The new Middleborough Station (located at 52 West Grove Street, Middleborough) will serve the commuter rail. 

**Fares**

The MBTA has determined that the fare structure for all South Coast Rail stations will be priced in Zone 8. This means that passengers will pay a full fare of $12.25 and a reduced fare of $6.

**Safety system testing complete**

Automatic Train Control (ATC) testing was completed in July, 2024 and [dispatch responsibilities were transferred to Keolis](https://www.mbta.com/news/2024-08-02/mbta-reaches-significant-milestone-south-coast-rail-keolis-has-assumed-dispatcher). Over 800 Positive Train Control (PTC) functions have been tested to ensure safety, reliability, and compliance. PTC system testing was completed in December 2024 and operations were transferred to Keolis on January 6, 2025.

**Construction complete**

All six stations -- located in Middleborough, East Taunton, Freetown, Fall River Depot, Church Street, and New Bedford -- were completed by September 2024. Stations are fully accessible. Certificates of occupancy have also been given for the New Bedford Station and the Wamsutta Layover Facilities.

**Operator training underway**

Qualification runs are currently underway to allow for operator training and route familiarity. Demonstration service is slated for early March. All part of the federal New Starts process, these remaining tasks represent the final phases of the testing and commissioning process.

Communities can expect to see more signage installed shortly, including station posters, route maps, directional street signs, and more.

March 25, 2025 marked the opening of the South Coast Rail commuter line, bringing service to Southeastern Massachusetts for the first time in 65 years.

Advisory Board staff had the great honor of riding the Fall River/New Bedford Commuter line from Boston to East Taunton for the Opening Day celebration. Hundreds of elected officials, state officials, and South Coast riders gathered on a rainy Monday to mark this milestone in Massachusetts public transportation.

![Image 1](https://i0.wp.com/mbtaadvisoryboard.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/IMG_2794-1.jpg?resize=1024%2C768&ssl=1)

![Image 2](https://i0.wp.com/mbtaadvisoryboard.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/IMG_4102.jpg?resize=1024%2C768&ssl=1)

Among the officials in attendance were Governor Healey, Lieutenant Governor Driscoll, Taunton Mayor O’Connell, Transportation Secretary Tibbits-Nutt, MBTA General Manager Eng. Speaking to attendees, officials praised the hard work of those involved with the decades-long project, and commended the rail’s positive impacts on local economies, sustainable commitments, and the quality of life of South Coast residents.

**For the Advisory Board, this extension of service marks the addition of two new members, and the AB warmly welcomes New Bedford and Fall River!**

![Image 3](https://i0.wp.com/mbtaadvisoryboard.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/IMG_2831.jpg?resize=1024%2C768&ssl=1)

![Image 4](https://i0.wp.com/mbtaadvisoryboard.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/IMG_2834.jpg?resize=1024%2C768&ssl=1)

The Fall River/New Bedford line will bring service to the communities of Taunton, Freetown, New Bedford, Middleboro, and Fall River. The service will run 32 trips between South Station and East Taunton on weekdays (15 trips on the Fall River line and 17 trips on the New Bedford Line) and 26 trips between South Station and East Taunton on the weekends. The trains will run every 70 minutes on weekdays and every 2 hours on the weekends. Riders will be charged Zone 8 fares with a full fare of $12.25 and a reduced fare of $6. To celebrate the new service, weekend service on the line will be free through April.
